Our hypothesis is that answers exhibiting a sentiment congruent with the sentiment of the question are more likely to be correct than those with contrasting or neutral sentiments. Beyond sentiment, we also recognize the importance of semantic word classes (or parts-of-speech) in understanding the nuances of language and identifying relevant phrases. By analyzing the syntactic roles and semantic categories of words within the question and potential answers, we can refine our ranking process and improve the accuracy of our predictions. To test our hypothesis, we developed a novel method that integrates sentiment analysis and semantic word classes into a ranking framework for why-questions. We applied this approach to a large-scale web corpus and evaluated its performance on a dataset of 850 why-questions. Our experimental results demonstrate a substantial improvement in precision at the top-1 answer – a 15.2% gain – compared to a state-of-the-art QA system that achieved top performance in a widely recognized Japanese non-factoid QA shared task (NTCIR-6). These findings highlight the value of incorporating seemingly intuitive aspects of human cognition, such as sentiment, into the design of QA systems. The remainder of this paper details our methodology, experimental setup, results, and concludes with a discussion of future research directions. Specifically, we will describe our approach to sentiment analysis, our semantic word class tagging method, and the integration of these features into our ranking algorithm. We will also analyze the impact of each component and examine the types of why-questions where our method performs best. Finally, we will explore potential avenues for extending this work, such as incorporating more sophisticated sentiment models and exploring the use of other cognitive biases in QA.

The burgeoning landscape of social media presents unique challenges and opportunities for natural language processing research. Among these, stance classification – identifying whether a piece of text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral attitude toward a particular topic – has gained significant traction. Initially explored in domains like Congressional debates and online forums (e.g., (Ishikawa & Councill, 2011; Sobala et al., 2013)), stance classification techniques have evolved considerably. Early approaches relied on traditional text classification methods, gradually transitioning towards more sophisticated structured output prediction models. Collective classification (Taskar et al., 2003) and sequence labeling (Jurafsky & Martin, 2008) are prominent examples of this evolution, aiming to leverage contextual information and dependencies within the data to improve prediction accuracy. This work focuses on the collective classification of stances on Twitter, a particularly dynamic and challenging environment given its high volume, short message length, and rapid evolution of topical discussions. Twitter, as a primary platform for real-time public opinion expression, offers a rich source of data for understanding sentiments and attitudes toward various entities, events, or policies. However, manually annotating large volumes of Twitter data for stance classification is a prohibitively expensive and time-consuming undertaking. This necessitates exploring weakly supervised learning techniques, where only a limited amount of labeled data is available. Traditional supervised learning paradigms typically require extensive labeled datasets to achieve satisfactory performance, restricting their applicability in scenarios where such resources are scarce. Addressing this limitation, our research investigates a relational bootstrapping approach to stance classification, leveraging the inherent network structure of Twitter to propagate labels and expand the training data. We employ hinge-loss Markov random fields (HL-MRFs) to model the relationships between tweets, users, and their interactions. This framework allows us to constrain the predicted stance labels of individual tweets and the latent stance preferences of users to be consistent with the underlying network topology. The core intuition behind our approach is that users who frequently interact and express similar opinions are likely to hold similar stances on a given topic. By explicitly modeling these relational dependencies, we can effectively “bootstrap” labels from a small set of initially labeled hashtags or phrases, enabling us to infer stances for a significantly larger number of unlabeled tweets. Furthermore, the enhanced training set derived from this relational bootstrapping process can be utilized to train any traditional linear text classifier, offering a valuable alternative when network information is unavailable or computationally expensive to integrate. Language modeling, the task of predicting the probability of a sequence of words, is a foundational problem in natural language processing. Traditional approaches often rely on n-gram models, which capture statistical co-occurrences of words, and neural network-based models, which learn distributed representations of words and their contexts. While effective, these methods often struggle to incorporate linguistic structure, such as syntax, which can significantly improve predictive power. Capturing both syntactic and semantic relationships between words simultaneously presents a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel language modeling approach, the Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM), designed to overcome this limitation. LTLM encodes the syntactic and semantic information of a sentence as a tree representing the roles of each word within the sentence. Unlike traditional tree language models that rely on pre-existing parse trees, LTLM learns these trees directly from the data, allowing it to discover latent syntactic structures that may not be captured by standard parsing techniques. The core of LTLM lies in its iterative tree learning process. During the learning phase, the model repeatedly refines the tree structure through node movements guided by Gibbs sampling. This process allows the model to explore a wide range of possible tree configurations, implicitly capturing the syntactic and semantic relationships between words. To facilitate this learning process, we have developed two distinct algorithms for tree inference given a sentence. The first algorithm leverages the efficiency of Gibbs sampling, enabling rapid tree construction, albeit without guaranteeing optimality. The second algorithm employs dynamic programming, a more computationally intensive approach, but which offers the guarantee of finding the most probable tree structure for a given sentence. We present a comparative analysis of these two algorithms, detailing their strengths and weaknesses in terms of speed and accuracy. Recognizing the well-established performance of n-gram models, we explore the integration of LTLM with a conventional 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney language model. Specifically, we combine these approaches using linear interpolation, allowing the model to benefit from both the statistical power of n-grams and the structural information encoded by the latent tree representation. We evaluate the effectiveness of LTLM through extensive experiments on both English and Czech corpora. Our results demonstrate significant perplexity reductions – up to 46% for English and 49% for Czech – compared to the standalone 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney language model. These substantial improvements highlight the potential of LTLM to enhance language modeling performance by incorporating latent syntactic and semantic structure. The remainder of this paper details the LTLM architecture, presents a thorough explanation of our tree inference algorithms, discusses the implementation specifics of our hybrid model, and concludes with a comprehensive analysis of our experimental results. We believe LTLM represents a promising step towards more linguistically informed and effective language modeling techniques. " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " "

Question answering (QA) systems have long sought to bridge the gap between natural language queries and factual knowledge. Traditional approaches often rely on leveraging vast corpora of unstructured text, enabling the acquisition of extensive knowledge but posing significant challenges for automated reasoning and accurate fact retrieval. Conversely, highly structured knowledge bases, such as RDF triples, provide a robust foundation for logical inference and precise querying; however, their construction typically demands extensive manual effort, hindering scalability and broad applicability. This inherent tension—the tradeoff between ease of acquisition and suitability for reasoning—has motivated research into intermediate formalisms that offer a degree of structure while retaining some of the flexibility of natural language. In this paper, we investigate the potential of tables as a compelling semi-structured knowledge representation for QA. Tables are ubiquitous in various contexts, appearing in web pages, reports, databases, and scientific papers. They inherently possess a structured organization – rows representing individual entities or instances, and columns denoting their corresponding attributes. This structure provides valuable cues for understanding the relationships between data elements, facilitating both knowledge extraction and reasoning. Unlike the dense and amorphous nature of unstructured text, tables offer a clearer delineation of entities and their properties, simplifying the task of identifying relevant facts and drawing logical conclusions. At the same time, unlike traditional knowledge graphs, tables are often readily available and can be extracted from numerous sources with relative ease. Their tabular format aligns well with the way humans naturally organize and process information, making them intuitive to both users and automated systems. However, to effectively leverage tables for QA, several challenges must be addressed. First, there is the need for substantial annotated data to train QA models capable of understanding the table structure and reasoning about its contents. Existing QA datasets predominantly focus on unstructured text, leaving a significant gap in the availability of datasets tailored to tabular knowledge. Second, effective QA models must be able to represent and exploit the semi-structured nature of tables, moving beyond simple text retrieval techniques that treat tables as flat sequences of words. They need to understand column labels, row semantics, and the relationships between entities described within the table. In this work, we tackle both of these challenges. We present a novel method for efficiently generating a large-scale QA dataset directly from tables using human crowd-sourcing, leveraging the inherent structure of tables to guide question and answer creation. Furthermore, we propose a feature-driven QA model that explicitly incorporates semi-structured information derived from the table’s layout and content, enabling it to reason over tabular knowledge. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms strong baselines, including a state-of-the-art unstructured retrieval model and a sophisticated Markov Logic Network, highlighting the promise of tables as a valuable resource for question answering. We posit that tables’ position between unstructured text and fully structured knowledge bases makes them uniquely suitable for enabling efficient reasoning through question answering. Through the remainder of the paper, we explore this position with attention to the methods for dataset creation and subsequent model training and evaluation. Through these investigations, we aim to demonstrate the effectiveness of employing tables as a knowledge base for question answering.

Phrase structure parsing, the task of assigning a syntactic tree structure to a sentence, remains a core problem in natural language processing. While significant progress has been made, particularly with the advent of lexicalized parsing (Collins, 2003), challenges remain, especially when dealing with morphologically rich languages. Traditional lexicalized parsers rely on a relatively simple, flat representation of lexical items, capturing information like word sense or lemma. However, morphologically rich languages present a nuanced challenge: a single surface form may represent a range of grammatical categories and features, requiring a more sophisticated lexical representation to capture this variability effectively. Furthermore, efficiency remains a critical consideration, as parsing large datasets or real-time applications demands scalable algorithms. Current state-of-the-art parsers, though highly accurate, often struggle to balance accuracy and speed, particularly when dealing with the complexities of morphologically rich languages like French. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a novel LR-based generalized lexicalized phrase structure parser. We draw inspiration from the LR parsing algorithms widely used in compiler construction, adapting their principles to the domain of syntactic parsing. The key innovation lies in our generalized lexicalized parser, which allows for a structured representation of lexical items. This structured representation goes beyond the typical single-value lexical representation used in standard lexicalized parsing, allowing us to encode a richer set of morphological and syntactic features associated with a word form. This is particularly beneficial for languages where a single surface form can have multiple interpretations based on its morphological properties. Our approach integrates this generalized lexicalization with a discriminative training framework (Collins, 2002), a technique proven highly effective for optimizing parsing accuracy. By jointly learning the parsing rules and the weights associated with different features, we achieve a synergistic effect, allowing the parser to leverage the structured lexical information to its fullest potential. Critically, we demonstrate that this combination of a structured lexical representation and discriminative weighting leads to state-of-the-art accuracy on French, a language characterized by its complex morphology. Furthermore, our LR-inspired parsing algorithm achieves more efficient parsing times than existing state-of-the-art French parsers, demonstrating a significant advantage in terms of computational efficiency. To illustrate the broader applicability of our approach, we also conduct experiments on English, a comparatively lexically poor language, and present a comparative analysis of the performance across both languages. The results highlight the benefits of our generalized lexicalized parser and its suitability for handling a diverse range of linguistic structures. We believe this work represents a significant step towards more accurate and efficient phrase structure parsing, particularly for morphologically complex languages. *** (Collins, 2003) refers to Michael Collins' seminal work on lexicalized parsing. The burgeoning field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) seeks to revolutionize learning experiences through personalized instruction, intelligent tutoring systems, and automated assessment. A crucial ingredient for achieving true AIEd capabilities is the ability to represent and reason with the explicit knowledge underlying academic disciplines. While vast amounts of educational content exist, extracting structured knowledge from these resources remains a significant challenge. Textbooks, in particular, represent a rich, authoritative, and conceptually organized source of knowledge, yet their unstructured nature hinders direct utilization by AI systems. This paper addresses this challenge within the domain of geometry, focusing on the extraction of axiomatic knowledge—the foundational rules and theorems that form the bedrock of geometric reasoning. Existing AI approaches to solving geometry problems often rely on rule-based systems or machine learning models trained on problem-solution pairs. However, these methods typically lack a deep understanding of the underlying geometric principles and struggle to generalize to novel problem scenarios. A more robust approach involves equipping AI systems with explicit knowledge about geometry – specifically, its axioms. Manually encoding such knowledge is time-consuming and prone to human error. Therefore, automated methods for knowledge acquisition from existing resources are essential. Previous work has explored knowledge extraction from various sources like Wikipedia or educational websites, but the structured and standardized nature of textbooks provides a particularly promising avenue for obtaining high-quality axiomatic knowledge. This research proposes a novel methodology for automatically harvesting axiomatic knowledge from math textbooks. Our approach aims to extract axioms in the form of Horn-clause rules, a standard representation suitable for logical reasoning. We move beyond simple keyword extraction by incorporating rich contextual and typographical features—such as sentence structure, surrounding terminology, and formatting—to identify statements with axiomatic significance. Crucially, we capitalize on the redundancy inherent in textbooks; geometric axioms are typically presented in multiple textbooks, often in a consistent order. By leveraging this shared ordering and cross-referencing information across different sources, we significantly enhance the accuracy and robustness of our knowledge extraction process. To validate our approach, we conduct a case study focused on extracting geometric axioms from a corpus of high school mathematics textbooks. We demonstrate that the harvested axioms, represented as Horn-clause rules, can be effectively integrated into a geometry problem solver, leading to improved performance and a deeper understanding of geometric reasoning compared to state-of-the-art solvers. The contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) A novel approach for extracting axiomatic knowledge from textbooks using contextual and typographical features; (2) A method to leverage redundancy and shared ordering across multiple textbooks to improve accuracy; and (3) An empirical demonstration of the effectiveness of harvested axioms in solving geometry problems, showcasing their potential to enhance AIEd systems. The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has long relied on treebanks – annotated syntactic structures of sentences – for training and evaluating various models, from parsing to semantic analysis. A crucial, yet often overlooked, component in leveraging these treebanks is the ability to systematically transform them. These transformations are required for various tasks, including correcting annotation errors, adapting treebanks to different syntactic theories, generating training data for specific parsing models, and performing cross-lingual transfer learning. However, the existing methods for describing these transformations are often ad hoc, scattered across different publications, and lack a formal, standardized language. This leads to significant challenges in reproducibility, implementation, and community collaboration. The textual descriptions of transformation rules found in the literature are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, and difficult to translate into executable code without introducing significant complexity and potential for error. The absence of a clear, well-defined transduction language for treebanks has hindered progress in several key areas. For instance, developing robust methods for automatically correcting annotation inconsistencies in large treebanks becomes considerably harder without a systematic way to define and apply the correction rules. Similarly, adapting treebanks annotated under one syntactic formalism to another – a common task in cross-lingual NLP – is hampered by the lack of a standardized framework. Moreover, creating synthetic training data by manipulating existing treebanks, a technique often used to augment limited data resources, becomes a laborious and error-prone process. In this paper, we address this critical gap by proposing a novel transduction language specifically designed for natural language treebank transformations. Our language aims to provide a clean, precise, and concise mechanism for describing transformations, moving away from the often-opaque and inconsistent textual descriptions prevalent in the literature. The language serves as the foundation for a tree transduction tool that allows users to express their desired transformations in a structured and unambiguous manner, significantly simplifying the implementation process. This tool enables easy, non-hard-coded execution of these transformations, promoting reproducibility and reducing the risk of errors. Furthermore, by offering a formal and standardized language, we hope to facilitate wider adoption and foster collaboration within the NLP community. Our ultimate goal is to solicit feedback and refine this language iteratively, ideally leading to a de facto standard for treebank transduction, thereby empowering researchers and practitioners with a powerful and accessible tool for effectively utilizing and manipulating valuable linguistic resources. We will demonstrate the applicability of our language and tool through examples drawn from common treebank transformation tasks described in existing NLP literature, illustrating its expressive power and ease of use. --- Hopefully, this meets your requirements! The demand for large, high-quality parallel corpora has long been a bottleneck in the advancement of statistical machine translation (SMT) and, increasingly, neural machine translation (NMT). While manually curated parallel datasets like Europarl and UN corpora remain invaluable, their size is inherently limited, and expanding them is a time-consuming and expensive endeavor. Consequently, web mining of parallel data has emerged as a promising avenue for rapidly augmenting existing resources and enabling translation for low-resource language pairs. Traditional web mining approaches often rely on leveraging readily available comparable corpora—collections of texts in different languages that cover similar topics—and then applying heuristics or statistical alignment techniques to identify potential sentence pairs. However, directly extracting parallel sentences from the vast and unstructured expanse of the web presents a significantly greater challenge, fraught with issues like noise, language identification errors, and the sheer volume of irrelevant data. This paper presents an empirical study exploring a novel approach to directly mining high-quality parallel data from the web, bypassing the need for initial comparable corpora. Our central hypothesis is that a carefully designed search strategy, combined with effective filtering mechanisms, can enable the extraction of reliable sentence pairs from web search results. Existing methods often struggle with the high noise level inherent in web-scraped data, resulting in parallel corpora that are either too small or contain a substantial proportion of erroneous sentence pairs, ultimately hindering the performance of downstream MT systems. We address this challenge by employing a two-pronged strategy: first, we formulate effective search queries designed to target web pages likely to contain parallel content, utilizing a “Learning to Rank” (LTR) approach to optimize query formulation; and second, we implement a robust filtering pipeline based on IBM Model 1 alignment to rigorously identify and discard noisy document pairs. This allows us to reduce the noise while retaining the potentially valuable parallel sentences found within the web pages. Critically, rather than simply presenting a new data extraction technique, we provide a comprehensive empirical evaluation of our methodology, demonstrating its impact on the performance of a statistical machine translation system. We hypothesize that our approach, by focusing on direct parallel sentence extraction and employing targeted query optimization and noise reduction, will significantly outperform existing web mining techniques and contribute to the creation of more effective training data for MT. The core contribution of this paper lies in demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of a direct web mining approach and in providing a detailed empirical analysis of the key components of our system. We believe that this work represents a significant step towards harnessing the vast potential of the web as a source of parallel data for machine translation. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTcyNTU4MjY0N119 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTcyNTU4MjY0N119 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTcyNTU4MjY0N119 -->

The generation of fluent and coherent text has been a long-standing goal in natural language processing. While significant progress has been made in areas like machine translation and text summarization, a persistent challenge remains: achieving sufficient variation in generated text. A critical aspect contributing to this issue is the consistency in the choice of referential forms—the pronouns, definite descriptions, and other linguistic devices used to refer to entities within a text. Human writers strategically vary their referential expressions to avoid monotony, maintain clarity, and signal relationships between entities. Current automatic text generation models, however, often default to the simplest or most frequent referential form, resulting in a stilted and unnatural reading experience. This paper addresses this limitation by exploring methods to introduce more variation in the choice of referential forms within automatically generated text. Our central motivation is to move beyond deterministic generation strategies and embrace a nondeterministic approach that explicitly models individual variation in how referents are expressed. We hypothesize that incorporating such variation will significantly enhance the perceived coherence and comprehensibility of generated texts. To investigate this, we present two novel models designed to capture these stylistic differences: a Naive Bayes model and a Recurrent Neural Network. We then conduct a user evaluation study where human judges assess the coherence and comprehensibility of the generated texts, comparing them both to the original references and a random baseline model. Our goal is to demonstrate that introducing controlled variation in referential form choices can lead to more natural and engaging automatically generated text, ultimately contributing to the development of more sophisticated and human-like language generation systems. Event extraction (EE) is a crucial task in natural language processing, aiming to identify and structure events described in unstructured text. These events, characterized by a trigger word and associated arguments (participants, time, location, etc.), form the foundation for building knowledge graphs and supporting downstream applications like question answering and information retrieval. While significant progress has been made in traditional EE on news articles and formal documents, applying EE to social media presents unique challenges. Social media platforms, such as Twitter and Facebook, are characterized by a distinct writing style—often informal, abbreviated, and lacking the rich contextual information found in more formal prose. This informality, coupled with the limited context within individual messages (e.g., a single tweet), makes it difficult for traditional EE systems to accurately identify and structure events. Consequently, existing event extractors designed for news often struggle to achieve satisfactory performance when applied directly to social media data. The core issue lies in the significant gap between the linguistic properties of social media messages and the data on which existing EE models are trained. Social media language frequently omits crucial context, relies on slang and abbreviations, and employs grammatical structures dissimilar to formal writing. This forces event extractors to make inferences with significantly less information, leading to errors in trigger identification and argument role labeling. Furthermore, the short-form nature of social media messages often doesn’t provide sufficient grounding to resolve coreferences and disambiguate event types. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach to cross-genre event extraction that leverages knowledge enrichment from more formal, contextualized sources. Instead of treating each social media message in isolation, our method incorporates information from external knowledge sources, specifically those representing higher-quality, more detailed accounts of events from news articles and other well-structured documents. By bridging the gap between social media language and established event knowledge, we aim to provide a social media event extractor with the necessary context and grounding to overcome the challenges posed by informal language and limited message content. Our approach doesn’t require any additional annotations related to the social media data itself; we leverage the readily available knowledge encoded within existing event corpora derived from news and formal documents. We demonstrate that this cross-genre knowledge injection significantly improves event extraction performance, achieving a substantial 15% absolute F-score improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods when applied to social media event extraction. This highlights the potential of knowledge-enriched approaches to effectively tackle the challenges of event extraction in informal, context-poor environments. We hypothesize that transferring knowledge from news articles to social media can bootstrap the event extraction process on social media by providing an external context to the short and informal messages. Through cross-genre knowledge enrichment, our proposed method can improve event extraction performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to cross-genre EE to exploit the complementary nature of social media and news data. We argue that such an approach can address the lack of context and informal nature of social media messages, permitting event extractors to boost their effectiveness.

Abstractive text summarization, particularly in the domain of news, has long been a challenging task in natural language processing. Unlike extractive summarization, which simply selects and concatenates existing sentences, abstractive summarization aims to generate novel sentences that capture the salient information in the source text. A key impediment to high-quality abstractive summarization lies in the ability to effectively represent the underlying events described in the source documents. Events, such as natural disasters, political elections, or business mergers, form the core of newsworthy content. A robust summarization system must be able to identify, understand, and accurately reproduce these events in a concise and coherent manner. We posit that events can be effectively modeled as collections of pattern clusters, where each cluster represents a specific event type (e.g., a protest, an acquisition) and each pattern within the cluster represents a distinct linguistic realization of that event (e.g., "X protested against Y," "X staged a demonstration against Y"). Previous work in multi-document abstractive summarization has often relied on heuristic-based approaches to extract these event patterns. While these methods provide a starting point, they suffer from limitations in their ability to capture the full range of linguistic expressions for a given event and are often brittle to variations in writing style. Inspired by recent advances in information extraction, we explore alternative strategies for event pattern extraction tailored for the abstractive summarization task. Specifically, we investigate both compression-based and memory-based methods, approaches that have not been extensively explored in the context of abstractive summarization. In this paper, we present a comparative analysis of three distinct event pattern extraction techniques: a traditional heuristic-based method, a novel compression-based approach, and a memory-based method leveraging a large corpus of parsed sentences. Our experiments reveal that the memory-based approach yields significantly more grammatical and informative sentences compared to the other two techniques. However, a critical challenge arises from the sheer scale of the search space: searching for matching parse sub-trees within a vast repository of hundreds of millions of parsed utterances is computationally expensive. To address this, we introduce an innovative data structure and a highly efficient search method that allows for rapid extrapolation from any given sentence to identify relevant parse sub-trees corresponding to stored utterances. This enables us to effectively leverage the power of the memory-based approach while mitigating the computational cost. The remainder of this paper details our methodology, experimental setup, results, and concludes with a discussion of future directions. Ultimately, we aim to contribute a novel and effective approach to event modeling that advances the state-of-the-art in abstractive text summarization. Narratives form the backbone of human communication, conveying experiences, sharing knowledge, and shaping cultural understanding. A key aspect of understanding narratives lies in recognizing recurring patterns of events – narrative schemas – and the roles that different participants play within these patterns. Traditional approaches to modeling narrative structure often rely on manually defined schemas and participant roles, a process that is both time-consuming and limited by the inherent biases of human design. This paper introduces a novel approach to uncovering these underlying narrative structures in an unsupervised manner, circumventing the need for supervised training data, hand-crafted knowledge bases, or pre-defined event or role categories. Existing research in event structure and semantic role labeling has largely focused on supervised methods, requiring extensive labeled datasets and complex feature engineering. While effective, these approaches struggle to generalize to new domains or languages where labeled data is scarce. Furthermore, previous attempts at unsupervised approaches often address event structure and semantic role learning separately, failing to exploit the inherent connections between them. For example, identifying a “trial” as a sequence of events is closely linked to understanding the roles of the judge, defendant, and lawyer within that trial. Our work tackles both the identification of narrative schemas and the definition of their participant roles in a unified, unsupervised framework. We propose a system that leverages the power of coreference resolution – the ability to identify which words or phrases refer to the same entities – to uncover recurring patterns in verb sequences. By tracking coreferring arguments across chains of verbs, our algorithm learns to extract both coherent event sequences, which we term narrative schemas, and rich semantic roles that define the participants involved. Anaphora resolution, the task of identifying the antecedent of a pronoun or other referring expression, is a cornerstone of natural language understanding. While traditional approaches have largely focused on coreference resolution, where the anaphor and antecedent represent the same real-world entity, a significant class of phenomena, known as associative anaphora, poses a distinct challenge. Associative anaphora, particularly prevalent in languages like Japanese, involves a non-coreferential relationship between the anaphor and its antecedent; the two entities are related conceptually or associatively, rather than being the same entity. Resolving this type of anaphora requires a deeper understanding of semantic relationships and world knowledge beyond simple identity checking. Failure to accurately resolve associative anaphora can significantly impede tasks such as machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Existing approaches to associative anaphora resolution often rely on hand-crafted rules or feature engineering, which are language-specific and difficult to generalize. Moreover, they frequently treat associative anaphora as a separate problem from coreference resolution, neglecting the potential benefits of a unified approach. In this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic model for associative anaphora resolution in Japanese. Our approach leverages the observation that associative anaphora can be viewed as a form of zero anaphora – a situation where an entity is implicitly referenced without explicit mention. By framing associative anaphora resolution in this manner, we can draw upon techniques developed for zero anaphora resolution and adapt them to handle the complexities of associative relationships. Crucially, our model utilizes automatically acquired lexical knowledge to capture these semantic associations, reducing the need for laborious manual feature engineering. The model estimates the probability of an antecedent being the referent of a given anaphor based on the lexical relationships between them, derived from large-scale corpora. Furthermore, we integrate the resolution of associative anaphora with coreference resolution, recognizing that these two phenomena often co-occur and can mutually inform each other. Experimental results on a benchmark Japanese corpus demonstrate that our model achieves high accuracy in resolving associative anaphora, and that performance is further improved when resolving associative and zero anaphora simultaneously. This unified approach offers a more robust and generalizable solution to this challenging problem, paving the way for more accurate and comprehensive anaphora resolution systems. Our contributions lie in the novel probabilistic framework treating associative anaphora as a type of zero anaphora, the exploitation of automatically acquired lexical knowledge, and the successful integration of associative and coreference resolution within a single model. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The construction of taxonomies – hierarchical structures that categorize concepts – is a fundamental task in knowledge representation and natural language understanding. Taxonomies enable a wide range of applications, including information retrieval, semantic search, and question answering. Manually constructing such taxonomies is a laborious and time-consuming process. Therefore, automatic taxonomy induction from text has emerged as a crucial research area, aiming to automatically learn hierarchical relationships between words and concepts. Traditional approaches to taxonomy induction often rely on heuristic rules or unsupervised clustering techniques, which frequently struggle to capture the nuanced semantic relationships required for accurate and comprehensive taxonomies. Recent efforts have explored supervised learning approaches, but these require extensive manually labeled data, which is difficult and expensive to obtain. This paper addresses the challenge of automatic taxonomy induction by proposing a novel structured learning approach grounded in probabilistic graphical models. Our key insight is that the structure of a taxonomy is inherently relational, meaning that the relationships between concepts (hypernymy – "is-a" – and siblinghood) impose constraints on the overall structure. We formulate taxonomy induction as a structured prediction problem, leveraging a probabilistic graphical model that elegantly incorporates both hypernymy and siblinghood information. To represent this relational information, we utilize heterogeneous evidence derived from large-scale Web resources, specifically n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts. These sources provide rich statistical patterns and semantic features that reflect the relationships between words and concepts. Efficiently inferring the optimal taxonomy structure within this graphical model is a computationally challenging task. To address this, we employ loopy belief propagation, a widely used inference algorithm for probabilistic graphical models, along with a directed spanning tree algorithm to optimize performance for the core hypernymy factor. Crucially, we employ discriminative learning to train our model. We extract sub-structures from the well-established WordNet taxonomy and use these as training data, aiming to learn a model that can accurately reproduce these known taxonomic relationships. Using adaptive subgradient stochastic optimization, we train the model to effectively capture the patterns encoded in the relational evidence, demonstrating the power of structured learning for this task. Our experimental results, evaluated on the task of reproducing sub-hierarchies of WordNet, showcase the significant advantages of our approach. We achieve a noteworthy 51% error reduction compared to a chance baseline, highlighting the effectiveness of our model in capturing taxonomic structure. Furthermore, the inclusion of non-hypernym-factored sibling features contributes to a 15% error reduction, demonstrating the importance of siblinghood information. Finally, a comparative evaluation against existing taxonomy induction methods reveals up to a 29% relative error reduction in ancestor F1 scores, solidifying the superiority of our structured learning approach. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm in machine translation, demonstrating substantial improvements over traditional Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) approaches (Bahdanau et al., 2014;Sutskever et al., 2014;Cho et al., 2014). The core of NMT lies in its ability to learn complex, non-linear mappings between source and target sequences using deep neural networks, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with attention mechanisms. Attention mechanisms allow the decoder to selectively focus on different parts of the input sequence when generating each target word, significantly enhancing translation quality and interpretability (Luong et al., 2015). While initial NMT models focused solely on textual input, the burgeoning field of multi-modal machine translation explores the potential of integrating information from other modalities, such as images, to improve translation performance. This is particularly relevant in scenarios where the input text is ambiguous or relies on visual context for accurate interpretation – for example, translating descriptions of objects or scenes. Existing research in multi-modal NMT has primarily explored the integration of visual features into either the encoder or the decoder, often through concatenation or attention mechanisms. However, a comprehensive investigation of different integration strategies and their relative effectiveness remains limited. Furthermore, many approaches struggle to fully leverage the global context provided by an image, often relying on localized features or restricting visual information to a single point in the translation process. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing a novel multi-modal NMT framework that incorporates global visual features into multiple aspects of both the encoder and decoder. Our core contribution lies in a systematic exploration of three distinct integration strategies: first, treating global image features as "words" appended to the source sentence; second, using the global features to initialize the encoder's hidden state, thereby informing the overall encoding process; and third, incorporating global features to initialize the decoder’s hidden state, guiding the initial stages of target language generation. Beyond the novel integration strategies, we investigate the impact of synthetic multi-modal, multilingual data augmentation on training NMT models. Generating such data is more cost-effective than gathering ground-truth parallel data, and previous work has confirmed the benefits of data augmentation in low-resource scenarios. However, the extent and effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation within multi-modal NMT remains an open question. Finally, we evaluate our models on the Multi30k dataset, a standard benchmark for multi-modal machine translation, comparing performance against different integration strategies and a strong PBSMT baseline. Our results demonstrate that incorporating global visual features into multiple parts of the NMT model consistently improves translation quality. Critically, we report new state-of-the-art results and demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge for the first time, that a purely neural model can significantly outperform a PBSMT model across all evaluated metrics on this dataset, highlighting the continued progress and potential of multi-modal NMT.

The burgeoning field of neural network-based natural language processing has witnessed remarkable success fueled, in large part, by the effective utilization of unsupervised pre-trained word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). A common practice involves using these pre-trained embeddings either as fixed representations or as initialization points for task-specific models. While effective, this approach can limit the model’s ability to adapt the word embeddings to the nuances of the target task. The embeddings, though generally informative, are not necessarily optimized for the specific characteristics of a given dataset or task. This is particularly relevant when dealing with specialized domains or complex relationships requiring fine-grained distinctions. The motivation for our work stems from the observation that fixed or minimally adapted embeddings may not fully exploit the potential of neural networks in capturing intricate patterns crucial for accurate classification. Specifically, we extend our classification model's task-specific loss with an unsupervised auxiliary loss operating at the word-embedding level. Our core idea is to encourage the model to learn word representations that reflect both task-relevant features – derived from the supervised loss – and more general linguistic features captured during the initial unsupervised pre-training. By jointly optimizing for both objectives, we aim to create a more robust and adaptable set of word embeddings that can significantly improve task performance. This dual-loss strategy allows the embeddings to simultaneously specialize to the specific task while retaining broader semantic understanding, creating a synergistic effect. We evaluate our proposed method on the challenging task of temporal relation extraction, focusing on narrative containment – identifying whether one event occurs before, during, or after another. Our results demonstrate that continued training of the embeddings on our proposed unsupervised objective, alongside the task objective, yields substantially improved task-specific embeddings, further bolstering the efficacy of our approach. We believe this work provides a valuable contribution to the field of neural network language processing by demonstrating the benefits of incorporating unsupervised learning at the word-embedding level for improved task performance. . The ability to simplify text while preserving its meaning is a core challenge in natural language processing (NLP), with significant applications ranging from text summarization to accessibility for language learners. Sentence compression, a specific form of text simplification, involves generating shorter versions of sentences that retain the core meaning. Traditionally, sentence compression has been investigated primarily within a monolingual setting, where a single language is considered. However, as multilingual NLP continues to advance, the need for cross-lingual methods is becoming increasingly apparent. This paper explores the relatively underexplored area of parallel sentence compression – the task of generating parallel compressions of parallel sentences. Consider a scenario where we have a dataset of news articles translated between two languages, such as English and German. Applying monolingual sentence compression to each language independently could yield compressed sentences that, while seemingly good within their respective languages, may no longer be perfectly aligned in terms of content or structure. Parallel sentence compression strives to address this limitation by jointly compressing sentences in both languages, ensuring that the compressed versions maintain a strong correspondence. Such an approach offers several potential benefits. It can facilitate the development of more robust and effective cross-lingual NLP systems, including machine translation (MT) and multilingual information retrieval. Parallel compressed sentences can serve as high-quality parallel data for training cross-lingual sentence manipulation tasks and can also reflect the relative importance of different sentence components across different languages. The task of syntactic analysis – determining the grammatical structure of a sentence – is a cornerstone of natural language understanding. While significant progress has been made in this area, particularly with the rise of neural network approaches, challenges remain, especially when dealing with morphologically rich and structurally complex languages like Chinese. Traditional approaches to syntactic analysis often rely on a pipeline architecture, where tasks such as word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and dependency parsing are performed sequentially. This pipeline approach, however, is vulnerable to error propagation: errors made in earlier stages of the pipeline can significantly impact the performance of subsequent stages, ultimately degrading the overall system accuracy. This issue is particularly pronounced in Chinese, where word segmentation is inherently ambiguous and tightly coupled with both POS tagging and dependency parsing. Recent advancements in neural networks have offered promise for addressing these limitations, yet fully joint models – approaches that perform all tasks simultaneously – have been relatively scarce, especially for Chinese. Existing neural approaches often focus on incorporating word embeddings as crucial features for dependency parsing, but effectively integrating these embeddings within a truly joint framework has proven difficult. Previous work has struggled to leverage the rich contextual information available across these interconnected tasks, limiting their ability to truly mitigate error propagation and achieve optimal performance. Moreover, many neural models still rely on hand-engineered features, hindering their adaptability and scalability to new domains or data. This paper introduces a novel neural joint model for Chinese syntactic analysis that directly tackles these challenges. Our approach unifies Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing into a single, trainable neural network. Crucially, we present the first fully joint neural models for Chinese analysis, designed specifically to prevent the error propagation inherent in pipeline architectures. To overcome the limitations of relying solely on word embeddings in a joint setting, we propose a novel architectural innovation: the use of character string embeddings alongside word embeddings. This allows our model to capture sub-word information and contextual dependencies that are vital for accurate Chinese word segmentation and subsequent parsing decisions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our joint models significantly outperform existing systems in word segmentation and POS tagging, and achieve competitive or superior accuracy in dependency parsing. Furthermore, we explore the efficacy of bi-LSTM architectures with a reduced feature set, showcasing the potential for efficient and effective joint modeling of Chinese syntactic analysis. The ability to organize knowledge into structured representations, known as ontologies, has become increasingly crucial for a wide range of applications, including knowledge discovery, information retrieval, and semantic web technologies. Ontologies explicitly define concepts (entities) within a domain and the relationships that exist between them, providing a semantic backbone for reasoning and integration of information. In many real-world scenarios, multiple ontologies describing the same or overlapping domains are developed independently by different groups or organizations. These parallel ontologies offer a rich source of knowledge but also present a significant challenge: how to effectively align the entities within these ontologies to unify and extend the existing knowledge base. Ontology matching, the process of identifying corresponding entities across different ontologies, is therefore a fundamental task in knowledge engineering. Traditionally, ontology matching approaches have relied on manual annotation, rule-based systems, or hybrid methods requiring a significant amount of domain expertise and labelled data—a costly and time-consuming undertaking. Recent advances in representation learning, particularly the development of powerful pre-trained word embeddings, have opened up new avenues for automating this process. These embeddings, capturing semantic relationships between words based on their contextual occurrences in large corpora, offer a promising foundation for unsupervised ontology matching. However, directly applying pre-trained word vectors to ontology matching is often suboptimal. Standard word embeddings are trained on general-purpose text and reflect general semantic knowledge, lacking specificity tailored to the nuances and vocabulary of a given ontology. There is a clear need for methods that can refine these pre-trained vectors to better represent ontological entities and their relationships, specifically for the task of ontology alignment. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing DeepAlignment, a novel and completely unsupervised approach to entity alignment. DeepAlignment leverages a refinement mechanism to adapt pre-trained word vectors, generating entity descriptions that are highly effective for ontology matching. The core innovation lies in the unsupervised refinement process, which operates without any explicit information about ontology matching during the vector adaptation. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepAlignment on several standard ontology matching benchmarks, achieving significant performance improvements compared to state-of-the-art methods. These results underscore the substantial benefits of incorporating representation learning techniques into ontology matching, paving the way for more automated and scalable knowledge integration solutions. Our work reveals a powerful synergy between pre-trained word vectors and task-specific refinement, opening new doors for unsupervised knowledge discovery and semantic integration. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTQ3Njg2MTAzOSwtMTEzMzY4NDU4OF19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTQ3Njg2MTAzOSwtMTEzMzY4NDU4OF19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTQ3Njg2MTAzOSwtMTEzMzY4NDU4OF19 -->

The increasing volume and complexity of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) present significant challenges for healthcare providers and researchers alike. A crucial component of EHRs is the collection of medical codes – standardized representations of diagnoses, procedures, and treatments, such as those from the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) and Current Procedural Terminology (CPT). These codes are essential for billing, reimbursement, quality reporting, and clinical decision support. However, the process of assigning these codes to clinical narratives—the free-text notes generated by clinicians during patient encounters—is a laborious, expensive, and often error-prone task. Manual coding necessitates extensive clinician time and expertise, leading to bottlenecks in healthcare workflows and potential inaccuracies that can impact financial and clinical outcomes. Furthermore, traditional coding processes often lack transparency, leaving clinicians without insight into the rationale behind specific code assignments. This lack of explainability can hinder trust in the coding process and limit its utility for broader clinical applications. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach for automating the prediction of medical codes from clinical text that emphasizes both accuracy and explainability. Existing literature has explored machine learning techniques for medical code prediction, with recent advances leveraging deep learning models. However, a key shortcoming of these approaches is their limited interpretability – they often function as “black boxes,” making it difficult to understand *why* a particular code was assigned. This is particularly concerning in a healthcare setting where transparency and accountability are paramount. Our work aims to bridge this gap by developing a model that not only achieves high prediction accuracy but also provides intelligible explanations for its decisions. We introduce an attentional convolutional neural network (CNN) designed specifically for this task. CNNs are well-suited for extracting local features from text, while the attention mechanism allows the model to selectively focus on the most relevant portions of the clinical note when predicting each code. This dual approach enables our model to effectively aggregate information across the entire document and highlight the specific segments that contribute most strongly to each code assignment. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of our method, achieving a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 score of 0.54 – both surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art approaches. Critically, we conduct a rigorous interpretability evaluation with a physician, who confirms that the attention weights generated by our model highlight clinically meaningful passages that justify the assigned codes. This validation underscores the potential of our approach to not only automate the coding process but also to enhance clinician understanding and trust in its outcomes. The proliferation of smartphones and the increasing adoption of voice assistants have dramatically altered how users interact with information. A significant portion of this voice-driven interaction revolves around local business discovery – users seeking nearby restaurants, shops, or services through voice commands. Consequently, local business directory assistance via voice search has become a crucial application, enabling users to quickly and easily access information relevant to their immediate surroundings. However, a persistent challenge in this domain lies in the relatively low accuracy of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems, particularly when transcribing business listing names. Business names are often lengthy, contain uncommon words or abbreviations, and are subject to significant speaker variability, contributing to recognition errors. These errors not only hinder the user experience but also impede the effectiveness of voice-based local search. Traditional approaches to enhancing ASR accuracy often rely on large, nationwide language models (LMs). While these models capture broad linguistic patterns, they struggle to effectively model the specific vocabulary and phonetic characteristics prevalent within localized business directories. A nationwide LM treats all business names equally, failing to account for the significant regional and geographic variations in business types and naming conventions. For instance, a district in Manhattan might have a high density of Italian restaurants with unique names, while a rural area might feature farms and agricultural businesses lacking such names. Consequently, a generic nationwide LM would perform poorly in accurately recognizing names specific to either location. To address this limitation, we propose a novel algorithm for generating geo-centric language models specifically tailored for local business voice search within mobile environments. Our approach overcomes the shortcomings of traditional nationwide LMs by leveraging geographic location data to construct localized language models, dynamically adjusting the scope of the model based on business density. This allows us to build highly accurate LMs focused on the specific business landscape of a given area. Furthermore, our algorithm is designed for efficiency; the generated LMs are pre-compiled and readily available, ensuring rapid recognition times. This is particularly important in the context of voice search, where users expect immediate results. In this paper, we detail our algorithm, demonstrating its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments using real-world spoken business listing name queries sourced from a business directory assistance service. The results demonstrate a compelling 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy and a remarkable 3-fold speedup in recognition time compared to a conventional nationwide language model. These findings underscore the significant potential of geo-centric language models to revolutionize the accuracy and speed of local business voice search, ultimately enhancing the user experience and realizing the full promise of voice-driven local discovery. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

In today's world, we are constantly bombarded with large numbers – billions of dollars in corporate earnings, millions of people affected by global events, astronomical figures representing government spending. While these numbers are meant to convey significance, they often fail to resonate with audiences, leaving them struggling to grasp their true magnitude. The human mind struggles to intuitively understand quantities far removed from our everyday experiences. Consider the statement "$131 million." What does that *really* mean? Is it a lot? How does it compare to something relatable? Existing methods of conveying scale, such as comparing to yearly salaries or household incomes, can be helpful, but they often rely on static comparisons and fail to capture the full spectrum of potential perspectives. This paper addresses this critical gap by introducing a novel task: automatically generating *perspectives*—short, compositional descriptions that contextualize numeric mentions and make them more readily understandable. Our goal is to move beyond simple comparisons and create descriptions that offer varied and relatable insights into the meaning of large numbers. For example, instead of just stating "$131 million is a large sum," our system might generate "$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period." This kind of contextualization fosters deeper understanding and greater engagement with the information. To achieve this, we present a system for automated perspective generation, breaking the task into two key stages: formula construction and description generation. The formula construction phase leverages a knowledge base to compose mathematical formulas that relate the target number to other numeric facts. We then rank these formulas based on factors such as familiarity (how common the comparison is), numeric proximity (how close the values are), and semantic compatibility (how logically related the concepts are). The description generation phase then takes the best-ranked formula and translates it into a natural language description using a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network. To facilitate research in this area, we also introduce a new dataset comprising numeric mentions extracted from news articles, each annotated with a set of rated perspectives. This dataset provides a valuable resource for training and evaluating perspective generation models. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing a substantial 15.2% F1 improvement over a non-compositional baseline in formula construction and a 12.5 BLEU point improvement in description generation, highlighting the benefits of our compositional approach. We believe this work represents a significant step toward making large numbers more accessible and meaningful to a wider audience. Introducing a new task of automatically generating short descriptions known as perspectives, e.g. "$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period". First, we collect a dataset of numeric mentions in news articles, where each mention is labeled with a set of rated perspectives. We then propose a system to generate these descriptions consisting of two steps: formula construction and description generation. In construction, we compose formulae from numeric facts in a knowledge base and rank the resulting formulas based on familiarity, numeric proximity and semantic compatibility. In generation, we convert a formula into natural language using a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network. Our system obtains a 15.2% F 1 improvement over a non-compositional baseline at formula construction and a 12.5 BLEU point improvement over a baseline description generation.

The burgeoning field of word embeddings has demonstrated remarkable success in capturing semantic relationships between words, facilitating advances in various natural language processing tasks. Traditional word embedding techniques, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), typically learn a single vector representation for each word, regardless of its multiple senses. This "one-sense" assumption can lead to a blurring of distinct meanings, hindering performance in tasks that require fine-grained semantic distinctions. Multi-sense word embeddings, which assign different vectors to different senses of a polysemous word, offer a potential solution. However, training these embeddings effectively presents significant challenges, particularly in leveraging both monolingual and cross-lingual information to enhance their quality. Recent approaches have explored various strategies for capturing word senses, including leveraging contextual information (Rei et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2017) or explicitly modeling sense inventories (Huang et al., 2016). Bilingual word embeddings, trained on parallel corpora, offer an additional avenue for improving sense representation. The assumption is that corresponding words in different languages often carry similar meanings, and exploiting this cross-lingual correspondence can lead to more robust and nuanced embeddings. However, effectively combining monolingual and bilingual data while explicitly modeling word senses remains an open challenge. Further, the computational complexity of directly mapping words across languages while also capturing fine-grained meaning can be prohibitive. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to bilingual learning of multi-sense word embeddings, utilizing a discrete autoencoder framework. Our model distinguishes itself by jointly learning an encoder and decoder, where the encoder leverages both monolingual and bilingual context to infer the appropriate sense for a given word. This sense inference then guides the decoder in predicting context words, allowing the model to learn sense-specific representations. Crucially, we employ a discrete latent space for representing word senses, enabling efficient exploration of the semantic landscape and facilitating the capture of distinct meanings. We argue that this discrete representation, combined with a joint training objective, allows our model to effectively exploit both monolingual and bilingual data, leading to improved multi-sense embeddings. Our experiments demonstrate that the word representations learned from bilingual data significantly outperform their monolingual counterparts across a range of evaluation tasks, even when cross-lingual information is unavailable at test time – a testament to the model’s ability to extract robust semantic information from parallel data. This highlights the potential of our approach for improving the quality and generalizability of multi-sense word embeddings across languages. 1 2 Related Work Traditional methods of word embedding (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) typically output one vector representation for each word, regardless of its polysemy. Subsequent work has attempted to learn multi-sense word embeddings through various approaches. Huang et al. (2016) explicitly modeled sense inventories using a knowledge graph-based approach. Yu et al. (2017) utilized contextual information to disambiguate word senses.

The notion that language reflects and shapes social dynamics is a cornerstone of sociolinguistics. Numerous studies have explored the relationship between social factors, such as power, and linguistic behavior. A particularly intriguing area is that of linguistic alignment—the tendency for speakers to converge in their linguistic features during conversations. It has been frequently asserted, and often observed, that individuals perceived as holding higher social power exert a stronger influence on their interlocutors, resulting in these lower-power speakers exhibiting greater linguistic convergence towards the higher-power speaker. This aligns with broader theoretical frameworks suggesting that power imbalances manifest in linguistic accommodation, where subordinate individuals adjust their language to mirror that of their superiors ( Giles et al., 1973). However, a critical examination of this established finding reveals a potential oversight: the influence of fundamental, low-level linguistic properties on alignment, which may inadvertently inflate or obscure the perceived impact of social power. While power dynamics undeniably shape social interactions, it's plausible that simpler, more immediate linguistic factors—such as utterance length, syntactic complexity, or lexical choices—may play a more deterministic role in driving alignment than previously recognized. This paper challenges the prevalent assumption that social power is a primary driver of linguistic alignment. We argue that observed alignment patterns are frequently attributable to these more basic linguistic features, and that the effect of social power, as traditionally measured, may be either overstated or even reversed when these features are appropriately controlled for. We meticulously investigate this claim through rigorous quantitative analysis, employing logistic regression models to dissect the interplay between social power and alignment across two distinct datasets. Our findings demonstrate that the purported power effect on alignment substantially diminishes, or even flips, once we account for readily observable linguistic characteristics. This suggests that alignment is more closely tied to the immediate, structural properties of utterances rather than the broader social hierarchy between speakers. We contend that future research on observational language data requires a broader perspective, moving beyond simplistic social factor analyses to incorporate a nuanced understanding of cognitive processes and the inherent linguistic constraints that govern conversational interactions. These often-overlooked cognitive factors, coupled with the grounding influence of low-level linguistic features, provide a more comprehensive and accurate explanation for observed patterns of linguistic alignment than the exclusive focus on social power has traditionally allowed. **References** Giles, H., Trudgill, P., & Newson, R. The accurate identification of predicate-argument structures—dependencies within a sentence that reveal which elements modify or relate to others—forms a cornerstone of numerous natural language processing applications. Tasks such as information extraction, question answering, and semantic parsing fundamentally rely on correctly discerning these relationships. While traditional syntactic parsing focuses on phrase structure, a significant challenge arises from *unbounded dependencies*, where a modifier can be arbitrarily far from the head it modifies, defying simple phrase-structure descriptions. These long-range dependencies are prevalent in natural language and often carry crucial semantic information, meaning their accurate recovery is essential for robust NLP systems. Existing approaches to dependency parsing often struggle to effectively handle unbounded dependencies, leading to incomplete or inaccurate interpretations of text. Categorial Grammar (CG) offers a compelling alternative to traditional phrase-structure grammars for representing syntactic structure. CG operates on the principle of composing words with associated categories that specify their syntactic behavior, using a small set of composition rules (functors and arguments) to construct increasingly complex sentences. This approach provides a relatively simple and uniform framework, facilitating the learning of grammatical structures. However, standard CG grammars can sometimes require a combinatorial explosion of categories to adequately encode grammatical constraints, hindering learnability. This paper introduces a novel approach to unbounded dependency recovery that leverages the strengths of CG while mitigating its limitations. We propose a *generalized categorial grammar* that combines the compositional benefits of CG with a strategy inspired by Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG). Specifically, our grammar aims to minimize the number of categories employed, restricting them to those necessary for enforcing grammatical constraints. This balanced approach allows for both the effective representation of unbounded dependencies and a manageable learning complexity. Crucially, the core of our grammar revolves around functor-argument relations, the very foundation of categorial composition, ensuring a consistent and interpretable semantic structure. To facilitate the application and evaluation of our generalized categorial grammar, we also present a novel reannotation system. This system efficiently converts existing syntactic resources, such as the Penn Treebank—traditionally annotated using Government and Binding (GB) theory—into our revised categorial representation. This allows us to build upon existing, valuable linguistic data for both training and evaluation. We then evaluate our grammar's performance on a standardized unbounded dependency recovery task, as defined by Rimell et al. (2009) and Nivre et al. (2010), demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately recovering these challenging dependencies. Our results offer a promising step towards more robust and accurate semantic interpretation systems capable of handling the complexities of natural language. Continuing work will investigate incorporating learned word embeddings and exploring probabilistic extensions of this grammar to further improve its performance and adaptability. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing has seen remarkable advances in information extraction (IE), traditionally a task focused on identifying entities and their relationships within a predefined schema. However, the rigidity of schema-driven IE limits its applicability to the vast, unstructured data streams characteristic of the modern digital landscape. Open Information Extraction (Open IE) emerged as a promising alternative, aiming to extract relational assertions from text without relying on a fixed set of relations, thereby enabling broader and more flexible knowledge discovery (Banko et al., 2006). While Open IE systems have demonstrated the ability to uncover diverse relationships within corpora, a critical challenge remains: the resulting extractions are often plagued by noise, redundancy, and a lack of coherence. Existing systems frequently produce assertions that are linguistically trivial, semantically uninformative, or simply inconsistent, hindering their utility for downstream applications such as knowledge graph construction and question answering. Current state-of-the-art Open IE approaches, including popular systems like TEXTRUNNER (Szabo et al., 2015) and WOE (Yih et al., 2015), primarily rely on syntactic patterns and learned models to identify relations. While these systems have achieved considerable progress, they often struggle to differentiate between genuinely meaningful relationships and spurious or unhelpful extractions. A fundamental limitation stems from the absence of explicit constraints guiding the extraction process, leading to a flood of superficial or incoherent assertions. This necessitates significant post-processing and filtering steps to salvage usable information, diminishing the efficiency and effectiveness of the overall IE pipeline. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces REVERB, a novel Open IE system that integrates two straightforward yet powerful constraints – syntactic and lexical – designed to improve the quality and coherence of extracted relations. We hypothesize that by incorporating these constraints directly into the extraction process, we can significantly reduce the volume of uninformative extractions while simultaneously enhancing the precision of meaningful assertions. Our work focuses specifically on binary relations expressed through verbs, a prevalent pattern in natural language. Through comprehensive experiments on standard datasets, we demonstrate that REVERB substantially outperforms existing Open IE systems, achieving more than double the area under the precision-recall curve compared to TEXTRUNNER and WOE. Moreover, a notable 30% of REVERB's extractions reach a precision level of 0.8 or higher, a stark contrast to the near-negligible performance of previous systems at this threshold. Finally, we provide a detailed error analysis of REVERB’s output, offering valuable insights into the remaining challenges and outlining promising avenues for future research and development in the domain of Open IE. This analysis will help further refine both REVERB and the field of Open IE at large, facilitating more accurate and useful extraction of knowledge from unstructured text.
