The identification of metaphors—the linguistic devices that imbue language with richness, nuance, and often, profound meaning—has long been a subject of fascination for linguists and a persistent challenge for computational systems. Automatic metaphor identification aims to address this challenge, enabling computers to not only detect metaphorical language but also to understand its function and impact. While significant progress has been made in recent years, existing approaches often rely on a combination of hand-crafted rules, extensive lexical resources, and complex semantic analyses. These methods, while effective in certain contexts, can be brittle, difficult to generalize to new domains, and require substantial human effort to develop and maintain. Furthermore, they often struggle with the inherent ambiguity and context-dependency that are hallmarks of metaphorical language. In this paper, we introduce a novel and fundamentally different approach to automatic metaphor identification that moves beyond the reliance on hand-crafted knowledge. Our system leverages the power of unsupervised learning, specifically verb and noun clustering, to identify metaphorical expressions directly from raw text data, starting with a relatively small seed set of manually annotated examples. This method distinguishes itself from prior work in its ability to autonomously discover metaphorical language without the need for pre-defined lexical features or intricate semantic models. The central hypothesis underpinning our approach is that metaphorical expressions, while semantically divergent from their literal counterparts, often share similar syntactic structures and patterns of verb-noun co-occurrence. By clustering verbs and nouns based on their contextual usage, we are able to identify groups of words that exhibit atypical or unconventional relationships, suggesting potential metaphorical usage. Unlike traditional rule-based or supervised approaches, our system's capacity to learn from the data itself offers a significant advantage in terms of adaptability and scalability. It can readily adapt to new corpora and domains without the need for substantial retraining or manual feature engineering. Moreover, the use of verb and noun clustering allows us to capture subtle nuances in metaphorical meaning that might be missed by more rigid semantic analyses. As far as we know, this is the first work to employ a purely unsupervised methodology for metaphor identification, demonstrating a promising avenue for future research in this area. Our experimental results, achieving a precision of 0.79, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and highlight its potential to significantly advance the field of computational metaphor analysis. . The digitization of printed books has rapidly accelerated in recent years, driven by initiatives like Google Books and the HathiTrust Digital Library. This has created unprecedented opportunities for digital humanities research, enabling large-scale analysis of literary trends, historical language usage, and the evolution of publishing practices. However, realizing the full potential of these digitized collections hinges on our ability to understand and represent the structural organization of books – moving beyond simply treating them as sequences of text pages. While optical character recognition (OCR) technologies have made the text itself accessible, the inherent structure of a book—its chapters, tables of contents, appendices, indices, and other elements—remains largely unrepresented in the digital format. Current methods often rely on rudimentary heuristics or metadata associated with the physical publication, which can be incomplete or inaccurate. This lack of structured information severely limits the applicability of these datasets for advanced analytical tasks. To address this gap, we introduce a new task: *book structure labeling*. This task involves the automated segmentation of a printed book into its constituent pages and the assignment of a predefined category to each page reflecting its structural role. Categories might include TABLE OF CONTENTS, PREFACE, CHAPTER, APPENDIX, INDEX, and so on. This structured representation allows for more sophisticated queries and analyses, such as identifying the prevalence of specific structural elements across different genres or time periods, or tracking how the organization of books has evolved over time. To facilitate research in this area, we have constructed a large-scale, manually annotated dataset designed specifically for book structure labeling. Our dataset comprises 294,816 pages extracted from 1,055 printed books, carefully sampled to provide a representative distribution of publications from the period 1750-1922. This historical range was selected to capture a period of significant change in both printing technology and publishing conventions. We detail the annotation process, emphasizing the guidelines and quality control measures implemented to ensure consistency and reliability. Furthermore, we present a comparative evaluation of several modeling approaches, ranging from simple rule-based systems to advanced deep learning architectures, assessing their performance on this new task. Our findings demonstrate that a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, augmented with a rich set of textual and visual features, achieves state-of-the-art results, attaining an overall accuracy of 95.8% and a class-balanced macro F-score of 71.4%. These results underscore the feasibility of automated book structure labeling and highlight the potential for unlocking valuable insights from digitized book collections. We believe that this work will serve as a foundation for future research in digital humanities, computational linguistics, and document understanding. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Data-Oriented Parsing (DOP) has emerged as a promising paradigm in syntactic parsing, challenging the traditional reliance on manually crafted grammar rules. DOP models, pioneered by Manning and Schütze (1999), leverage the statistical patterns observed directly within a treebank to guide the parsing process. Instead of defining grammar rules explicitly, DOP parsers learn to recognize and combine syntactic fragments extracted from the treebank, effectively constructing parse trees from these observed patterns. This approach offers several advantages, including reduced reliance on linguistic expertise and the potential to capture subtle syntactic variations that might be missed by handcrafted grammars. However, a key challenge in DOP lies in managing the complexity of the fragment space. Treebanks, even those of moderate size, contain a vast number of potential fragments, many of which are infrequent or idiosyncratic. Consequently, naïve DOP approaches can suffer from data sparsity and overfitting. To mitigate these issues, several DOP variants have been proposed, each employing different strategies for fragment selection and combination. Some approaches focus on restricting fragment size, while others prioritize fragments with high statistical support. In this paper, we present a novel DOP approach, dubbed Double-DOP, designed to achieve accurate and efficient parsing with a compact and representative set of syntactic fragments. Like other DOP models, our parser operates on syntactic fragments of arbitrary size derived directly from a treebank. However, a crucial distinction of our approach is the stringent criterion we impose on fragment selection: we consider only those fragments that appear at least twice within the treebank. This seemingly simple constraint has profound implications. Firstly, it dramatically reduces the size of the fragment space, mitigating the data sparsity problem and enabling the efficient training of probabilistic models. Secondly, by focusing on frequently observed fragments, we ensure that the selected fragments are representative of the underlying grammatical structure, forming a robust symbolic backbone for the parser. Importantly, our model avoids the need to manually craft any grammar rules; the grammar is implicitly learned from the data through the frequent co-occurrence of syntactic fragments. To facilitate parsing, we employ a transform-backtransform approach, elegantly enabling the application of standard Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) technology. This allows for straightforward implementation and, crucially, ensures that our results are easily replicable and comparable to existing parsing methods. Our evaluation, conducted using standard Parseval metrics on a widely used Penn Treebank, demonstrates that our best Double-DOP model achieves performance on par with many state-of-the-art parsers. Beyond its competitive accuracy, Double-DOP offers several complementary benefits. It provides a simple and interpretable generative probability model that directly reflects the frequency of observed syntactic fragments. Furthermore, it ensures an explicit representation of larger units of grammar, moving beyond the focus on individual words and phrases that often characterizes traditional parsers. This explicit representation can be valuable for downstream applications such as grammatical error correction and semantic parsing. The remainder of this paper details the Double-DOP approach, including the fragment selection process, the transform-backtransform mechanism, and the probabilistic model. We then present our experimental results and discuss the implications of our findings.

The burgeoning field of transfer learning has revolutionized machine learning, enabling models to leverage knowledge gained from one task or domain to improve performance on another. Traditional supervised learning approaches necessitate extensive, labeled data for each new task - a prohibitive burden in many real-world scenarios. Transfer learning circumvents this limitation, offering the promise of efficiently adapting models to novel domains with limited or no labeled data. While significant progress has been made in transfer learning, a particularly challenging frontier remains: cross-domain text classification with multiple source domains and, crucially, disparate label sets. Many practical applications, especially those dealing with diverse data sources and evolving user needs, face precisely this challenge. Consider, for instance, classifying social media posts across several platforms—each using distinct hashtag conventions and community-specific jargon—where the categories of interest (e.g., product feedback, customer support requests, brand mentions) might not neatly align across platforms. Similarly, applying classification models across different newsgroups within the 20 Newsgroups dataset presents issues, as the specific topics discussed and the terminology employed will inevitably vary. Existing transfer learning techniques often assume that the label spaces between the source and target domains are aligned or at least partially overlapping. Approaches like domain adaptation and multi-task learning struggle when faced with vastly different label sets, where categories have different meanings or granularities, or when the number of categories differs significantly. Simply mapping labels between domains is often insufficient due to semantic nuances and contextual differences. This disconnect limits the effectiveness of current transfer learning methods in these complex, real-world scenarios. To address this gap, we present a novel transfer learning algorithm specifically designed for cross-domain text classification with multiple source domains and disparate label sets – a first-of-its-kind approach to our knowledge. Our core idea revolves around identifying and selectively aggregating transferable knowledge from multiple source domains, even when their label sets are non-overlapping or semantically distinct. Instead of directly transferring models or features, we focus on identifying *instances* from the source domains that exhibit characteristics most beneficial for learning the target domain task. These instances, effectively a ‘selective’ subset of the source data, are then used to construct an auxiliary training set tailored for the target domain. This auxiliary set facilitates learning a model specifically targeted towards effectively generalizing across diverse domains and disparate label structures. The effectiveness of our proposed algorithm is rigorously validated through experiments conducted on real-world social media data and the widely-used 20 Newsgroups dataset, demonstrating significant performance gains over established baseline methods. Our results showcase the promise of this approach for enabling robust and efficient cross-domain text classification in challenging scenarios previously intractable with existing techniques. Coreference resolution (CR), the task of identifying all expressions that refer to the same entity in a text, is a fundamental problem in natural language understanding. Accurate coreference resolution is crucial for a wide range of downstream NLP applications, including information extraction, machine translation, and question answering. While substantial progress has been made in monolingual CR, particularly with the rise of machine learning approaches (e.g., McDonald et al., 2000; Schäfer et al., 2004), the problem of cross-lingual coreference resolution has received considerably less attention. Cross-lingual CR aims to resolve coreference links across different languages, a task becoming increasingly important with the growing availability of multilingual data and the need for cross-lingual information access. The challenge lies in bridging the linguistic gap between languages – differing syntax, morphology, and discourse conventions – to accurately identify corresponding entities. Existing attempts at cross-lingual CR have largely relied on projection-based methods (Langford et al., 2002; Potsdam CR Project, 2007), which project coreference chains learned in one language onto another. However, these approaches tend to be limited by the quality of the word alignment and struggle to generalize beyond closely related languages. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a novel machine learning approach to cross-lingual coreference resolution, specifically focusing on the resolution of English pronouns in a bitext of English and Czech. To our knowledge, this represents the first work to directly apply a machine learning approach to this challenging cross-lingual CR problem. Our core idea is to leverage the complementary information available in the Czech side of the bitext to enrich the feature set of a standard monolingual English CR system. We hypothesize that features derived from the Czech text, such as word translations and syntactic relationships, can provide valuable cues for identifying corresponding pronouns and resolving coreference links. Furthermore, we introduce a supervised pronoun aligner designed to learn better alignments between English and Czech pronouns than traditional word alignment tools like GIZA++ (Venugopalan and Klein, 2002). The results of our experiments demonstrate that our cross-lingual CR system consistently outperforms both a monolingual English CR system and a cross-lingual projection system, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach and the potential of leveraging parallel data for cross-lingual coreference resolution. Community Question Answering (CQA) platforms have become invaluable resources for information seeking, offering a vast repository of user-generated knowledge. A crucial component of effective CQA systems is answer selection—the task of identifying the most relevant and helpful answer from a pool of candidate responses to a given question. This task is central to improving the user experience, reducing information overload, and enhancing the overall utility of CQA forums. While significant progress has been made in answer selection, existing approaches often overlook key structural characteristics of questions common in real-world CQA environments. In many CQA platforms, questions are not presented as monolithic blocks of text but are structured into distinct parts: a concise subject line that summarizes the core inquiry and a more detailed body that provides context and elaboration. Previous research in answer selection has largely treated these question components equally, concatenating the subject and body into a single representation before feeding it into a model. This approach, while simple, risks diluting the critical information contained in the subject, which often serves as a succinct distillation of the user's need. The body, while providing valuable detail, can also contain extraneous information that may not be directly relevant to identifying a suitable answer. We hypothesize that leveraging the inherent relationship between the question subject and body—specifically, recognizing the subject as the primary driver of relevance—can significantly improve answer selection performance. To this end, we introduce Question Condensing Networks (QCN), a novel neural network architecture designed to explicitly model the subject-body relationship in CQA questions. QCN departs from traditional approaches by prioritizing the question subject in its representation and strategically incorporating information from the body based on its semantic similarity and disparity with the subject. This allows the model to effectively condense the body's details, retaining only the information that is most pertinent to answering the question as defined by the subject. Our proposed QCN model employs a mechanism for aggregating body information guided by a comparison to the subject, enabling the system to focus on relevant details while filtering out noise. We evaluate QCN on two widely used CQA datasets, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art answer selection models. This result underscores the importance of considering the structural nuances of CQA questions and highlights the potential of targeted architectural designs for enhancing performance in this crucial task. The field of machine translation (MT) has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by advances in neural network architectures and training techniques. A central focus of this progress has been the optimization of MT systems against evaluation metrics designed to approximate human judgment of translation quality. Traditional approaches to MT optimization typically rely on single-objective methods, seeking to maximize a single metric, most commonly BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). While effective, these single-objective methods often exhibit limitations, as a given metric captures only a subset of the complex factors that contribute to high-quality translation. For instance, BLEU, while widely used, is known to correlate imperfectly with human judgments, particularly for languages with different word order or morphological structures. It can also be gamed, rewarding systems that produce n-gram overlap rather than truly fluent and semantically accurate translations. Furthermore, the landscape of MT evaluation metrics is diverse, with different metrics—such as TER (Snover et al., 2006), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and chrF (Popović, 2015)—each emphasizing different aspects of translation quality. TER, for example, penalizes translation errors like deletions, insertions, and substitutions, while METEOR incorporates stemming and synonym matching to better account for lexical variation. A natural question arises: Can we leverage the complementary strengths of these diverse metrics to improve the overall quality of MT systems beyond what is achievable with a single-objective approach? Existing attempts to combine multiple metrics often involve ad hoc linear combinations, where each metric is assigned a weight and the weighted sum is used as an overall objective function. However, these methods suffer from a key drawback: the selection of appropriate weights is often arbitrary and requires careful tuning, which can be a computationally expensive and subjective process. Moreover, such linear combinations can mask trade-offs between different metrics, as improvements in one metric may come at the expense of another. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel multi-objective optimization approach for machine translation based on the well-established theory of Pareto optimality. This framework allows us to simultaneously consider multiple metrics without needing to predefine a specific weighting scheme. By identifying a set of Pareto-optimal solutions—those that cannot be improved in one metric without sacrificing performance in another—we enable a more nuanced and comprehensive optimization process. Our approach is remarkably straightforward to implement on top of existing single-objective optimization methods such as MERT (Zou et al., 2005) and PRO (Cherry and Lin, 2012), requiring minimal modifications to the underlying training procedure. We demonstrate empirically that our Pareto-based approach consistently outperforms ad hoc linear-combination alternatives, achieving improved translation quality across a range of metrics. Moreover, we discuss the crucial issue of metric tunability and show that our multi-objective framework is more robust and effective in incorporating new MT evaluation metrics during the optimization process, providing a pathway for continuous improvement as the field of MT evaluation evolves.

The ability to understand and predict human behavior in strategic interactions is a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence. While significant progress has been made in areas like game playing and decision-making, accurately modeling the nuanced interplay between communication and action remains a key frontier. In many real-world scenarios, individuals engage in dialogue to influence each other’s decisions, forging agreements or attempting to gain an advantage. This presents a compelling opportunity to leverage natural language processing techniques to gain deeper insights into human strategic reasoning. This paper focuses on the intersection of strategic conversation and game theory, specifically addressing the problem of predicting trades in a win-lose game. We investigate this problem within the context of *The Settlers of Catan*, a popular board game involving resource acquisition and trading. Catan’s trading dynamics create a rich environment for studying negotiation – players must strategically assess the value of resources, anticipate their opponents’ needs, and articulate their demands to secure favorable exchanges. The game's win-lose nature, where one player’s gain often comes at another’s expense, further heightens the strategic complexity, demanding careful consideration of both immediate and potential future outcomes. Previous research has explored the use of game theory to analyze Catan, but these approaches typically assume static player preferences. This is a significant limitation, as preferences in Catan are rarely fixed – they evolve based on resource scarcity, development card acquisition, and the perceived strategies of opponents. Our work departs from these static models by incorporating the richness of player communication. We analyze negotiation dialogues collected during Catan gameplay, employing them to construct a *dynamic* partial model of each player's preferences. This model isn't a complete representation of every possible trade, but rather a probabilistic assessment of likely desired outcomes, revised in real-time based on the evolving conversation. Using principles from game theory – specifically, identifying equilibrium trading moves – we then predict the trades players will ultimately execute. The core idea is that players, acting rationally, will tend to gravitate towards trades that represent a stable equilibrium point, given their current preferences and the perceived preferences of others. To evaluate our approach, we compare it against four carefully chosen baselines, including models based on static preference estimations and simple frequency counts. Our experimental results demonstrate that tracking how preferences evolve through the dialogue – a key contribution of our method – and reasoning about equilibrium moves are both crucial for achieving accurate trade prediction. This highlights the importance of incorporating dynamic preference modeling and game-theoretic reasoning when analyzing strategic conversations. Ultimately, this work contributes a novel framework for grounding strategic conversation in predictive models, paving the way for a deeper understanding of human decision-making in interactive environments. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0Sw__":eyJcaWQiOiJzY2hpc3RvcmUiLCJzbWl0IjoiMzEiLCJkYXRhIjp7ImV4cGVydGVkIjoidGhlIiwibmFtZSI6Ikdyb3VuZ2luIHN0cmluZyBDb25jZXB0YW5nOiBWb3luZ2EgU3RyaW5nIEFuc3dlciJ9fX0= -->

Spoken dialogue systems (SDS) have seen remarkable progress in recent years, fueled by advancements in areas such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language understanding (NLU). However, a critical bottleneck remains in the natural language generation (NLG) component, which is responsible for crafting the system’s responses. The quality of these responses profoundly impacts both the usability and the perceived naturalness of the overall SDS, significantly influencing user satisfaction. Currently, many deployed SDS rely on NLG systems built upon rule-based or template-based approaches. While these systems offer a degree of control and predictability, they frequently suffer from a rigid and stylised output, lacking the nuanced variation and adaptability characteristic of human conversation. Moreover, rule-based systems are notoriously difficult to scale; the creation and maintenance of extensive rulesets become increasingly burdensome as the system’s scope expands across multiple domains and languages. The limitations of traditional NLG methods have motivated significant research into statistical approaches, particularly those leveraging neural networks. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and their more sophisticated variants like Long Short-term Memory networks (LSTMs), have demonstrated impressive capabilities in sequence-to-sequence tasks, including NLG (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). However, a significant challenge in applying LSTMs to NLG within the context of dialogue systems is ensuring semantic control – that is, generating responses that accurately reflect the underlying dialogue state and fulfil specific communicative goals. Prior efforts have often relied on hand-engineered features or complex training regimes to achieve this control, adding to the system's complexity and limiting its adaptability. In this paper, we propose a novel statistical language generator based on a semantically conditioned LSTM architecture designed specifically for spoken dialogue systems. Our approach distinguishes itself through its simplicity and efficiency. We demonstrate that our LSTM generator can effectively learn to generate natural and informative responses directly from unaligned data, eliminating the need for complex sentence planning stages often required by traditional NLG pipelines. The model is trained end-to-end using a straightforward cross-entropy loss function, jointly optimizing both sentence planning (selecting appropriate content) and surface realisation (constructing grammatically correct and fluent sentences). Furthermore, we leverage the inherent probabilistic nature of LSTMs to introduce language variation by sampling different output candidates, resulting in less repetitive and more engaging dialogue. The design allows for easier scaling and transfer capabilities with minimal hand-engineering required. We present empirical results from two distinct dialogue domains, demonstrating that our proposed method outperforms several established NLG baselines. Crucially, human evaluations revealed that our LSTM-based system generated responses deemed more informative and natural, and was consistently preferred by human judges overall. Our work contributes a practical and effective approach to semantically controlled NLG, paving the way for more human-like and adaptable spoken dialogue systems. *** (Sutskever et al., 2014) - This is a citation to the original Seq2Seq paper. The longstanding goal of natural language processing is to bridge the gap between human language and machine understanding. A crucial step towards this goal is the development of robust and accurate semantic parsers – systems capable of translating natural language utterances into formal, machine-interpretable representations of their meaning. While significant progress has been made in semantic parsing, particularly with the rise of neural network approaches, challenges remain, especially when dealing with the complexities of discourse and anaphoric relations. Natural language rarely presents information in a self-contained, atomic manner. Instead, communication builds upon previous utterances, referencing and connecting ideas across multiple sentences. This interconnectedness requires a parser to not only understand the immediate meaning of an utterance but also to maintain a coherent model of the ongoing discourse. Traditional semantic parsing methods often struggle to adequately capture these dynamic aspects of language, limiting their applicability in open-domain scenarios. To address these limitations, we investigate the construction of formal meaning representations based on Discourse Representation Theory (DRT). DRT, introduced by Kamp and Reyle (1993), provides a powerful framework for analyzing the semantic structure of discourse, explicitly modeling anaphoric relations and the evolution of the discourse context. A central construct in DRT is the Discourse Representation Structure (DRS), a graph-like structure that represents the entities, relations, and conditions introduced by each utterance and how they relate to the overall discourse state. Generating accurate DRSs is a complex task, requiring a parser to reason about both the syntactic and semantic properties of the input text and the evolving discourse context. This paper introduces a novel open-domain neural semantic parser designed specifically to generate DRSs. Our approach distinguishes itself through a structure-aware decoding process, which meticulously decomposes the complex task of DRS generation into a sequence of manageable stages. First, the model predicts the fundamental architectural structure of the DRS, outlining the relationships between its core components. Subsequently, it predicts the conditions within that structure — the predicates and relations that define the meaning of the utterance. Finally, and crucially, the model predicts the referents – the variables that track entities and concepts across the discourse. To facilitate training and enable effective learning of these complex dependencies, we develop a method to transform DRSs into tree structures, providing a more amenable format for neural network processing. Experimental results on the Groningen Meaning Bank (GMB), a widely recognized benchmark dataset for DRT parsing, demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms competitive baselines, representing a substantial advancement in the state-of-the-art for DRS parsing and a major step towards more sophisticated and context-aware semantic understanding. We believe our structure-aware approach has broad implications for building more robust and adaptable semantic parsers capable of handling the intricate nuances of real-world discourse. </br> References: Kamp, H., & Reyle, U. The development of statistical machine translation (SMT) has been largely driven by the pursuit of improved automatic evaluation scores, particularly BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). Traditional SMT tuning, however, typically focuses on optimizing a single evaluation metric, often BLEU, which can lead to a narrow focus and potential trade-offs. While improvements in BLEU scores are desirable, they do not always correlate directly with human judgments of translation quality. Recent years have seen a growing awareness of this limitation, with the introduction of additional metrics such as RIBES (Ramírez et al., 2015), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and TER (Snover et al., 2006), designed to capture different aspects of translation quality beyond n-gram overlap. Consequently, there’s a need for effective methods that can simultaneously optimize performance across multiple evaluation metrics. This multi-metric optimization (MMO) presents a significant challenge, as improving one metric can often negatively impact another, leading to a complex optimization landscape. Existing approaches to MMO broadly fall into two categories: weighted tuning and Pareto-optimization. Weighted tuning involves assigning weights to different metrics and optimizing a combined score, but determining appropriate weights can be difficult and often requires manual tuning or heuristics. Pareto-optimization, on the other hand, aims to identify a set of solutions that are non-dominated, meaning that no solution is better than another across all metrics. While Pareto-optimization provides a richer set of solutions, it still requires a mechanism for selecting a single, representative solution from the Pareto frontier. Moreover, many MMO approaches struggle to scale effectively to high-dimensional metric spaces and complex model architectures. In this paper, we investigate novel approaches to MMO within the context of statistical machine translation, focusing on ensemble decoding methods as a means to effectively combine multiple Pareto-optimal solutions. We argue that rather than selecting a single Pareto-optimal solution, an ensemble of solutions can often yield superior performance, leveraging the strengths of each individual model without sacrificing performance on any single metric. Central to our approach is the concept of Pareto-optimality, which provides a principled framework for identifying and combining solutions that exhibit balanced performance across multiple evaluation metrics. Our contributions are threefold: First, we propose several novel tuning methods tailored for MMO, including techniques that explicitly search for Pareto-optimal ensemble models. Secondly, we introduce a new algorithm specifically designed for multi-metric optimization that leverages ensemble decoding to combine Pareto-optimal solutions. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both single and multiple reference datasets, demonstrating simultaneous gains across a range of metrics (BLEU, RIBES) without significant degradation on others – a stark contrast to traditional single-metric tuning. Furthermore, our human evaluation results provide compelling evidence that MMO, as facilitated by our ensemble tuning approach, leads to demonstrably better translation quality compared to optimizing solely for a single metric. This reinforces the importance of considering a broader range of evaluation criteria when optimizing machine translation systems.

The ability to automatically extract structured knowledge from unstructured natural language text is a cornerstone of modern information processing. Among various knowledge extraction tasks, event detection stands out as a crucial step, involving the identification of event mentions within text and their classification into predefined event types (e.g., birth, marriage, protest). Such events form the building blocks of structured knowledge bases, enabling a wide range of applications including news analysis, knowledge discovery, and question answering. Traditionally, event detection has relied on feature engineering and conditional random fields (CRFs) to achieve decent performance. However, the burgeoning success of deep learning has led to a paradigm shift, with neural network models increasingly dominating the state-of-the-art (Li et al., 2016; Nguyen and Allen, 2016; Zeng et al., 2017). While neural networks have undeniably demonstrated their superiority, a critical gap remains in our understanding of the relative strengths and weaknesses of different neural architectures specifically tailored for event detection. Existing studies often focus on incremental improvements over a single model or a limited comparison of a few architectures, neglecting a rigorous and comprehensive empirical evaluation. This lack of rigorous comparison hinders the community’s ability to select the most appropriate model for a given scenario and impedes further advancements in the field. The primary motivation of this work is to address this gap. We recognize that the effectiveness of a neural network model is not solely determined by its architecture, but also by factors such as random initialization, training-validation-test data splits, and hyperparameter tuning. These factors introduce inherent variability in the reported performance, potentially masking subtle differences between otherwise comparable models. To obtain a more reliable and insightful assessment, we believe that a rigorous empirical evaluation framework is necessary, involving multiple runs with varied initializations and data splits. In this paper, we present such an evaluation framework and apply it to the widely used ACE2005 dataset. Furthermore, to contribute a meaningful addition to the existing pool of models, we propose a novel GRU-based model that explicitly incorporates both syntactic information and temporal structure. Our model leverages an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the importance of different words and their contextual relationships, capturing both the immediate meaning and the broader narrative flow surrounding event mentions. Through extensive experiments under diverse conditions, we demonstrate that our proposed model achieves competitive performance compared to other leading neural network architectures, providing a valuable benchmark and a deeper understanding of the landscape of neural network approaches for event detection. Specifically, we analyze the impact of different configurations and highlight the factors that contribute to robust and reliable event detection performance. We expect our findings to guide future research in this area and promote the development of more effective and reliable event detection systems. The task of named entity recognition (NER) has achieved considerable success in recent years, with sophisticated models capable of identifying and classifying entities such as people, organizations, and locations within unstructured text. However, a crucial subsequent step – named entity canonicalization – remains a significant challenge. Canonicalization, in essence, involves mapping diverse mentions of the same real-world entity to a single, standardized representation, often referred to as a “canonical” entity. For example, “Barack Obama,” “Obama,” and “President Obama” all refer to the same individual. Efficient and accurate canonicalization is vital for downstream applications like knowledge graph construction, information retrieval, and question answering, where consistent entity representations are essential for meaningful analysis. Despite its importance, canonicalization often struggles with the inherent ambiguity of natural language, variations in mention phrasing, and the presence of noisy or incomplete data. Traditional approaches often rely on rule-based systems or simple agglomerative clustering techniques, which often prove brittle and struggle to generalize to unseen data or handle the complexities of real-world mention patterns. Previous statistical approaches have often focused on isolated mention-to-entity mappings, neglecting the valuable context surrounding these mentions or failing to incorporate nuanced linguistic features. This paper introduces a novel probabilistic model designed to address these limitations and significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of named entity canonicalization. Our model departs from existing approaches by integrating several key innovations. Firstly, we explicitly incorporate entity context – the surrounding text – as a critical factor in determining whether two mentions refer to the same entity. Secondly, we leverage surface features of mention tokens, such as capitalization, part-of-speech tags, and morphological information, to capture subtle distinctions between different mention forms. Perhaps most notably, our model incorporates first-order dependencies among attribute-parts, recognizing that certain combinations of attribute values are more likely to correspond to the same entity. Finally, we explicitly model noise in the data, acknowledging that mentions can be inaccurate or incomplete and developing mechanisms to mitigate their impact on the canonicalization process. We employ a transductive learning framework, exploiting a small set of seed mentions and a larger collection of unannotated mention tokens to perform Bayesian inference and conditional estimation, thereby leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data to achieve optimal performance. We evaluate our model and its components extensively on two distinct datasets derived from political blogs and sports news, demonstrating its superior performance compared to a simple agglomerative clustering baseline and previous state-of-the-art approaches. Our results underscore the effectiveness of our probabilistic model in capturing complex mention patterns and accurately resolving entity ambiguities, paving the way for more robust and reliable knowledge graph construction and information extraction systems. The prospect of predicting stock market movements has captivated investors and researchers alike for decades. While traditional financial models rely heavily on historical price data and economic indicators, the rise of social media has opened up a new avenue for gathering potentially valuable information. The sentiment and discourse surrounding companies expressed on platforms like Twitter (now X) could provide early signals about market trends, potentially offering a competitive edge. However, forecasting stock movements remains a formidable challenge. The financial market is inherently stochastic, characterized by unpredictable fluctuations and influenced by a myriad of factors. Furthermore, we are tasked with making temporally-dependent predictions, meaning that each prediction is conditioned on past observations, further complicating the task given the chaotic nature of the data. Existing approaches often struggle to reconcile these complexities, particularly in effectively integrating textual data with the inherent noise and dynamic patterns of historical price series. Many earlier efforts in this domain have explored using sentiment analysis of tweets to predict stock prices, often employing discriminative models or topic modeling techniques. However, these approaches frequently overlook the stochastic nature of the market and the intricate temporal dependencies that govern stock movements. Discriminative models, for instance, can struggle to capture the underlying probabilistic structure of the data, while topic modeling often fails to adequately represent the nuanced and dynamic sentiment expressed in tweets. This motivates the need for a more sophisticated approach that can explicitly model stochasticity and temporal dependencies while effectively fusing textual and numerical information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel deep generative model specifically designed for stock movement prediction. Our model uniquely integrates text signals from Twitter and historical price data within a unified framework, effectively exploiting both sources of information for superior prediction accuracy. Crucially, we leverage neural variational inference to tackle the intractable posterior inference inherent in generative models, facilitating efficient training and adaptation. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid objective function incorporating temporal auxiliary information, allowing the model to flexibly capture the often complex predictive dependencies between past events and future stock movements. We validate the efficacy of our proposed model on a newly curated stock movement prediction dataset, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and highlighting the potential of deep generative models for this challenging task. The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed remarkable advances in recent years, largely fueled by deep learning techniques. However, despite this progress, many NLP tasks remain intrinsically linked to the underlying syntactic structure of language. While traditional approaches to incorporating syntactic information often rely on parsing at runtime – a computationally expensive operation – recent work has explored methods to leverage syntactic knowledge without incurring such a performance penalty. This poses a significant challenge: how can we effectively encode syntactic information into models for semantic tasks without the overhead of real-time parsing? Many semantic tasks, such as semantic role labeling (SRL), frame alignment, and coreference resolution, inherently rely on understanding the relationships between words and phrases within a sentence, relationships that are fundamentally encoded in its syntactic structure. Directly incorporating parse trees into neural models has proven difficult, often leading to overfitting and poor generalization. Furthermore, reliance on a parser introduces a bottleneck—errors in parsing directly propagate to the semantic task. Existing methods for incorporating syntax often fall into two categories: those that rely on syntactic features hand-engineered to be fed into models, and those that incorporate tree-based structures directly at runtime. The former suffer from the labor-intensive and often sub-optimal nature of feature engineering, while the latter are constrained by the computational cost of parsing. Inspired by research in developmental psychology, which suggests that children initially learn language through loosely structured syntactic "scaffolds" before developing a complete understanding of grammar, we propose a novel approach called *syntactic scaffolding*. Our method aims to embed syntactic information into semantic models during training, leveraging a treebank to learn syntactic representations, while avoiding expensive parsing at inference time. The core idea of syntactic scaffolding is to train a model with a multitask objective that simultaneously predicts the semantic label and learns a representation of the syntactic structure. This allows the model to implicitly capture syntactic information without explicitly relying on a parser. Specifically, we introduce a novel architecture that encourages the model to learn meaningful connections between syntactic constituents and semantic roles, enabling it to leverage syntactic patterns to improve semantic understanding. By exploiting the syntactic structure observed in a treebank during training, our model learns to anticipate and utilize syntactic patterns without the runtime overhead of parsing. We present empirical results demonstrating that this approach significantly improves performance on a range of semantic tasks, including PropBank semantic role labeling, frame semantics alignment, and coreference resolution, achieving competitive results compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Our results indicate that syntactic scaffolding provides a robust and efficient way to incorporate syntactic information into semantic NLP models, offering a valuable contribution to the ongoing effort to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics. We believe this work opens new avenues for leveraging syntactic knowledge in a computationally efficient manner, paving the way for more robust and accurate semantic understanding systems. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, enabling increasingly fluent and accurate translations between languages. However, a persistent challenge lies in accurately handling lexical ambiguity – the phenomenon where a single word in the source language can have multiple meanings (senses) that require different translations in the target language. Traditional SMT systems often treat words as monolithic entities, ignoring the crucial role of word sense in determining the appropriate translation. This simplification can lead to suboptimal translations, particularly in languages with rich morphology and subtle semantic distinctions. The core premise underlying this work is simple: the correct translation of a word is fundamentally dependent on the sense in which it is used within a given context. Previous attempts to incorporate word sense information into SMT have largely focused on adapting word sense disambiguation (WSD) techniques. These approaches typically treat WSD as a pre-processing step, assigning senses to words *before* translation. While seemingly intuitive, this reformulation suffers from a critical limitation: it disregards the inherent fluidity and contextual nature of word senses. Pre-defining senses and applying them rigidly can artificially constrain the translation process, preventing the decoder from adapting to subtle nuances in the input sentence. Furthermore, many WSD methods rely on manually curated dictionaries and sense inventories, lacking the adaptability to handle specialized domains or evolving language use. In this paper, we introduce a novel sense-based translation model that directly integrates word sense information into the SMT decoding process. Our approach differs significantly from previous reformulations of WSD in that it embraces the natural, context-dependent nature of word senses. Rather than imposing predefined senses, we propose a method for automatically learning sense clusters for words in the source language using a nonparametric Bayesian topic model. This allows the model to discover groupings of words that exhibit similar distributional characteristics, effectively representing different senses based on the textual context in which they appear. Subsequently, we leverage these inferred senses within a maximum entropy classifier, enabling the decoder to select the most appropriate translation for each source word based on its contextually derived sense. This allows for a more nuanced and flexible translation process. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on a large-scale Chinese-to-English translation task. Our results demonstrate that the proposed sense-based translation model significantly outperforms both baseline SMT systems and previous approaches that reformulated WSD. The improvements underscore the potential of dynamically learning and leveraging word sense information to enhance the accuracy and fluency of machine translation. We believe that our contributions represent a significant step toward more robust and human-like machine translation systems. Finally, we highlight the following novel aspects of our work: (1) a broad-coverage sense tagger based on a nonparametric Bayesian topic model for automatic sense cluster learning, and (2) an SMT model that integrates these inferred senses for sense-aware translation decoding. We anticipate that this line of research will inspire further innovation in incorporating semantic information into statistical machine translation models. The field of distributional semantics has revolutionized our understanding of word meaning in computational linguistics. Pioneering work by Harris (1954) established the foundational principle that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. This principle has been formalized and implemented in numerous computational models, ranging from simple co-occurrence counts to sophisticated neural embeddings like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014). These textual distributional models have proven remarkably successful in capturing semantic relationships between words, enabling applications like word similarity estimation, analogy detection, and even aspects of semantic inference. However, a crucial limitation of these models lies in their purely linguistic grounding. They derive meaning solely from textual co-occurrence, neglecting the rich perceptual experience that shapes human understanding. Humans do not simply learn the meaning of “red” from reading sentences containing the word; we also experience the color red directly through vision. This raises a fundamental question: are we capturing the full spectrum of word meaning by relying only on textual data? This paper explores this question by investigating the possibility of grounding distributional semantics in perception. We argue that incorporating visual and multimodal information can enrich our computational models of word meaning, particularly for words with strong perceptual correlates. Previous work has begun to explore this avenue, utilizing image retrieval techniques to build “visual lexicons” (Bruni et al., 2011) and constructing distributional models based on the co-occurrence of words and images (Frome et al., 2013; Rohrbach et al., 2011). However, these early approaches often relied on relatively simple image representations. With the recent advancements in computer vision, particularly the rise of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large-scale image datasets like ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), we now have the tools to build significantly more sophisticated visual and multimodal distributional models. Our research aims to leverage these advancements to build computational models of word meaning that are perceptually grounded. We construct visual distributional models using state-of-the-art computer vision techniques to represent images and learn word embeddings based on the co-occurrence of words and visual features. We then compare these visual models to traditional textual models across a range of tasks, including assessing semantic relatedness and evaluating their ability to capture the meaning of specific word categories. Our findings reveal that while visual models, in general, may not yet surpass textual models in capturing broad semantic relatedness, they demonstrate a remarkable ability to model the meaning of words with strong visual correlates – such as color terms – even in challenging scenarios involving nonliteral usage. We also provide evidence that visual and textual information tap into different facets of word meaning, and that combining them through multimodal approaches often leads to improved performance, effectively painting distributional semantics in “technicolor.” --- References (Placeholder - full references would be included in a paper) * Bruni, E., Tran, X., Kulesza, A., & Reichert, V. Scope learning, the task of identifying the linguistic spans over which a particular cue phrase exerts its semantic influence, is a critical component of many natural language understanding tasks. Accurately determining scope is crucial for tasks like question answering, textual entailment, and sentiment analysis, as it directly impacts the meaning derived from a sentence. Traditional approaches to scope learning often rely on complex, hand-engineered rules or sophisticated deep learning models, which can be computationally expensive and challenging to adapt to new domains or cue types. Recent advancements have explored the use of machine learning techniques, however, effectively capturing the structural relationships between cues and their scope remains a non-trivial challenge. This paper proposes a novel and unified framework for scope learning that leverages simplified shallow semantic parsing. Our core idea is to recast the scope learning problem as a structured prediction task, where the cue phrase is treated as a predicate and its scope is mapped onto the constituents within the sentence, effectively defining the arguments of that predicate. This perspective allows us to utilize the strengths of parsing techniques to discover the structural relationships vital for accurate scope determination. Unlike traditional parsing approaches that aim for full syntactic analysis, we employ a *simplified* shallow semantic parsing method, focusing on identifying relevant constituents directly related to the cue phrase, and avoiding the complexities of full syntactic representation. This streamlined approach significantly reduces computational overhead while retaining key structural information. The parsing technique implemented in our framework identifies constituents dominated by the cue phrase, mapping these constituents as arguments to the cue predicate. For instance, in the sentence “John didn’t go to the store,” the cue ‘didn’t’ (negation) would be the predicate, and the phrase "go to the store" would be its primary argument, representing the scope of negation. This structured representation provides a clear and concise depiction of the cue-scope relationship, facilitating efficient scope learning. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on the BioScope corpus, a widely used benchmark dataset for scope learning. Our evaluation demonstrates that incorporating structural information through this parsing approach significantly enhances scope learning accuracy compared to methods that ignore syntactic structure. Notably, our parsing framework substantially outperforms state-of-the-art chunking-based approaches, underscoring the importance of structured information in scope learning. We also observed that our simplified shallow semantic parsing method provides a practical and efficient alternative to more complex parsing techniques, while still capturing the necessary syntactic details. While our initial evaluation focuses on negation and speculation scope learning, our framework’s architecture is inherently portable to other types of scope learning. The core principle of treating the cue as a predicate and mapping its scope to constituents remains applicable across various cue types and linguistic phenomena. Therefore, this work provides a solid foundation for a unified approach to scope learning that can be easily adapted and extended to address a broader range of scope learning challenges. We believe that this simplified shallow semantic parsing approach provides a valuable contribution to the field, offering a more efficient, interpretable, and adaptable framework for scope learning.

The task of disfluency detection—identifying and segmenting speech errors, hesitations, and other non-fluent speech phenomena—is a crucial component of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and spoken language understanding. Accurate disfluency detection can significantly improve the performance of downstream applications such as transcription, summarization, and dialogue systems. Traditional approaches to disfluency detection have largely relied on handcrafted features and conditional random fields (CRFs), often requiring extensive linguistic expertise and feature engineering. While these methods have achieved reasonable performance, they struggle to capture the complex and long-range dependencies inherent in spoken language, particularly the subtle grammatical and semantic cues that indicate disfluency. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly the emergence of sequence-to-sequence models and attention mechanisms, offer a promising alternative for addressing these limitations. Sequence-to-sequence models excel at capturing contextual information and modeling dependencies between input and output sequences, while attention mechanisms allow the model to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of the input when generating the output. Inspired by these developments, this paper proposes a novel neural attention-based model for disfluency detection, framing the task as a sequence-to-sequence problem. Our approach leverages a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BI-LSTM) network to encode the input sentence, followed by a neural attention mechanism that functions as a “pointer,” selecting an ordered subsequence of the input words to represent the disfluency-free sentence. By explicitly modeling the relationships between words and allowing the model to “attend” to different parts of the input, we effectively capture long-range dependencies and create a more accurate representation of the sentence’s grammatical structure. This approach moves beyond simply classifying each word as fluent or disfluent and instead aims to reconstruct a grammatically correct version of the input. We rigorously evaluate our model on the widely used English Switchboard test set, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with an F-score of 86.7%. Furthermore, we extend our investigations to an in-house annotated Chinese dataset and observe a significant improvement in performance compared to a baseline CRF-based approach, highlighting the broad applicability of our model across different languages. Our results suggest that neural attention models offer a powerful and effective solution for disfluency detection, surpassing traditional methods in both accuracy and efficiency. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) remains a core challenge in natural language processing, impacting a wide range of downstream tasks including machine translation, information retrieval, and text understanding. The fundamental problem lies in determining the correct sense of a polysemous word within a given context – a task humans perform effortlessly, yet proves surprisingly difficult for machines. However, the creation of these annotated datasets is a costly and time-consuming endeavor, severely limiting the scope and scalability of these methods. Furthermore, the senses defined in these datasets may not always align perfectly with how language is used in diverse real-world contexts. Recent advancements have explored unsupervised and semi-supervised techniques to alleviate the reliance on labeled data. However, supervised methods, when properly leveraged, continue to offer strong performance. The critical bottleneck remains the representation of contextual information in a way that effectively distinguishes between different word senses. While features like the surrounding words (bag-of-words, n-grams), part-of-speech tags, and syntactic dependencies have proven valuable, they often struggle to capture the subtle nuances that differentiate senses. The limitations of these traditional features underscore the need for novel approaches to incorporate broader contextual information without incurring substantial annotation costs. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a new feature class for supervised WSD: *web-scale selectors*. Our central hypothesis is that words appearing in similar local contexts across different, large-scale, unannotated corpora can serve as strong indicators of a word’s sense. We leverage the vast resources of the Web – essentially, treating the Web as a massive collection of diverse corpora – to identify these selectors. The core idea is that if a particular word consistently appears alongside a specific set of surrounding terms in various textual contexts, it’s likely that the word is being used with a consistent meaning. This approach sidesteps the need for human annotation while simultaneously enriching the contextual information available to the sense classifier. We present a method for extracting these selectors from unlabeled Web-scale corpora and integrating them as features in a supervised sense classifier, specifically employing Support Vector Machines (SVMs). The increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs) has created unprecedented opportunities for analyzing patient histories and improving healthcare outcomes. The remarkable ability of humans to understand and generate language relies heavily on the principle of semantic compositionality – the idea that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. This principle, foundational to linguistic theory and computational semantics, posits a systematic relationship between the meaning of a phrase or sentence and the meaning of its individual words. While largely accepted, the degree to which semantic compositionality holds true across languages and across different linguistic structures remains a subject of ongoing investigation. German compound nouns, in particular, offer a compelling testbed for exploring the extent and limitations of semantic compositionality. The inherent complexity of German compounds presents a significant challenge. While many exhibit a straightforward, predictable meaning—where the meaning of the whole is readily derivable from the components—others display non-compositional behavior, exhibiting idioms, metaphorical extensions, or semantic shifts that defy simple summation. Understanding the nature and frequency of these compositional violations is crucial for building effective Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems capable of accurately interpreting and generating German text. Recent advancements in vector space models, such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and fastText, have provided powerful tools for representing words as dense vectors capturing semantic relationships. These representations have proven invaluable in various NLP tasks, but their ability to accurately reflect compositional meaning, especially in morphologically complex languages, remains an open question. Can we leverage these distributed semantic representations to “reverse-engineer” the meaning of a compound noun, by accurately reconstructing its vector representation from the representations of its constituent parts? This paper addresses this question by examining the performance of several composition models on a large dataset of German compound nouns. We investigate established models proposed in the literature, exploring their strengths and weaknesses in capturing the semantic relationships within German compounds. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, relatively simple composition model and demonstrate its superior performance on our dataset. Our study aims to provide empirical evidence for the extent of semantic compositionality in German and to contribute to the development of more robust and accurate computational models of language understanding. Ultimately, this research seeks to shed light on the fundamental cognitive processes underlying language comprehension and to improve the effectiveness of NLP applications dealing with the complexities of German morphology. The availability of high-quality treebanks is crucial for numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly those involving syntactic analysis. Treebanks, which provide manually annotated syntactic structures for a corpus of text, serve as invaluable resources for training and evaluating syntactic parsers, informing linguistic research, and facilitating the development of various downstream applications like machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. While substantial progress has been made in treebanking for languages like English, German, and French, the development of comprehensive and versatile treebanks for languages with significantly different syntactic structures, such as Chinese, presents unique challenges. Existing Chinese treebanks, such as the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB), have been instrumental in advancing Chinese NLP research. However, they often adopt a single syntactic representation, typically focusing on dependency structures. This reliance on a single view can limit the flexibility and utility of the treebank for certain applications and hinder a more holistic understanding of Chinese syntax. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel multi-view annotation framework for Chinese treebanking. This framework leverages dependency structures as the foundational view, acknowledging their established role in Chinese syntactic analysis. Crucially, it also supports seamless conversion to phrase structures while minimizing information loss. This dual representation allows researchers and developers to explore syntax from different perspectives and utilize the treebank for a broader range of tasks. The ability to easily transition between dependency and phrase structure representations is particularly important given the distinct theoretical perspectives and practical advantages associated with each formalism. Moreover, a multi-view treebank facilitates the development of more robust and versatile parsers that can effectively handle the complexities of Chinese syntax, which exhibits characteristics of both analytic and synthetic structures. Under this proposed framework, we have constructed a multi-view Chinese treebank, which we are releasing as PMT 1.0 (Project Multi-view Treebank). The initial release comprises 14,463 sentences and will be made freely available to the research community, fostering collaboration and accelerating progress in Chinese NLP. To validate the efficacy of our multi-view framework, we implemented an arc-standard transition-based dependency parser. Central to our evaluation is the incorporation of phrase structure features – derived from the phrase structure view of the treebank – into the parser. Experimental results demonstrate that these additional features significantly enhance the parser's performance on dependency parsing tasks. Beyond parsing, we further assessed the utility of our treebank and parser in the context of dependency-to-string machine translation. The results demonstrate that our approach can achieve comparable performance to the widely-used Stanford Parser trained on the established CTB 7.0, highlighting the potential of our multi-view framework to contribute to advancements in Chinese NLP applications. This paper details the design and implementation of our multi-view annotation framework, describes the construction of PMT 1.0, and presents the experimental results supporting the effectiveness of our approach. . . . . . . . . . .

The vast expanse of the World Wide Web represents an unparalleled repository of human knowledge, answering countless questions directly. However, even this immense corpus remains incomplete; many answers lie hidden, waiting to be revealed through logical inference. Consider the simple statement, “Paris is the capital of France.” From this, one can infer that “the capital of France is in Europe.” While the second statement isn't explicitly stated, it is readily derivable. But where do these inference rules—the foundational building blocks enabling such reasoning—originate? This question lies at the heart of a longstanding challenge in knowledge representation and reasoning: how to automatically acquire the rules that govern relationships between concepts. This paper tackles this challenge directly, exploring the problem of learning inference rules from the unstructured text of the Web in an unsupervised and, crucially, domain-independent manner. Existing approaches to knowledge acquisition often rely on curated datasets or expert-defined rules, limiting their applicability and scalability. Others focus on extracting only explicit facts, missing the rich tapestry of implicit knowledge embedded within natural language. Systems like TEXTRUNNER (Popescu et al., 2003) excel at extracting facts directly stated in the text, but their ability to uncover hidden knowledge is inherently constrained. We hypothesize that the Web, despite its inherent noise and ambiguity, contains a wealth of information suitable for learning general inference rules. To this end, we introduce SHERLOCK, a novel first-order learner designed to capture this implicit knowledge. SHERLOCK autonomously acquires over 30,000 Horn clauses—a concise and expressive logical formalism—directly from the Web. A key innovation within SHERLOCK is its rule scoring function, which departs from traditional approaches that often struggle with the Web’s inherent complexities. We leverage the concept of Statistical Relevance (Salmon, 1971) to assign scores to potential rules. Statistical Relevance, in essence, measures the extent to which the presence of one event (the antecedent of a rule) reliably predicts the occurrence of another (the consequent). This framework proves remarkably effective in navigating the ambiguous, noisy, and incomplete nature of Web extractions, allowing SHERLOCK to identify robust and meaningful rules. Our experimental results convincingly demonstrate the power of this approach. Inference over the rules learned by SHERLOCK discovers three times as many facts as TEXTRUNNER (at a precision of 0.8), showcasing the significant advantage of learning inference rules over simply extracting explicit facts. This work represents a significant step towards realizing the full potential of the Web as a source of knowledge, moving beyond explicit statements to unlock the power of implicit relationships. . Unlike existing approaches that focus on directly predicting entity types from limited training data, FINET adopts a fundamentally different strategy. We recognize that even in short texts, a wealth of semantic information can be extracted and leveraged. FINET’s core innovation lies in its multi-stage architecture, which utilizes a cascade of "extractors" to generate a wide range of candidate types, spanning both explicitly mentioned types and more subtle, implicit ones. These extractors operate without requiring any direct supervision, allowing us to avoid the pitfalls of data scarcity. This allows for a significantly more precise characterization of entities than has previously been possible, enabling downstream applications to benefit from a deeper understanding of entity semantics. N-gram language models have long served as a cornerstone of statistical natural language processing, proving remarkably effective in tasks ranging from speech recognition to machine translation. However, a well-documented limitation of these models is their inability to effectively incorporate contextual information beyond the immediate n-gram sequence. The core assumption—that the probability of a word depends solely on the preceding n-1 words—ignores the broader semantic landscape, often referred to as "topic," that significantly influences language use. Recognizing this deficiency, researchers have explored various extensions to integrate topic information into n-gram models, aiming to capture a more nuanced understanding of language. Wallach (2006) pioneered a Bayesian topic language model, offering a promising avenue for leveraging topic structure. This work, while groundbreaking, faced challenges related to data sparsity, particularly when dealing with higher-order n-grams and a partitioning of all n-grams into exclusive topics. This exclusivity can unduly restrict the model's flexibility and prevent it from capturing the nuanced interplay between topic and n-gram probabilities. Building upon the foundation laid by Wallach, this paper addresses these limitations with two key innovations. First, we investigate novel prior distributions designed to mitigate the sparsity problem inherent in partitioning n-grams into discrete and exclusive topics. Traditional approaches often struggle when faced with limited data for specific topic-ngram combinations, leading to unreliable probability estimates. Our exploration of alternative priors aims to regularize the model, promoting more robust and generalizable predictions even in data-scarce scenarios. Existing approaches often treat topic assignments as static, hindering the model’s ability to explore the vast probability space and discover optimal configurations. Our blocked sampler, specifically designed for higher-order n-grams, efficiently enables the reassignment of multiple n-grams simultaneously, accelerating convergence and facilitating a more comprehensive search for higher-probability topic-ngram arrangements. Furthermore, our empirical findings demonstrate the efficacy of a model where not all parts of a document are assigned a distinct topic, allowing for a more flexible and realistic representation of document content.
